question: A data engineer needs to ingest from both streaming and batch sources for a firm that relies on highly accurate data. Occasionally, some of the data picked up by the sensors that provide a streaming input are outside the expected parameters. If this occurs, the data must be dropped, but the stream should not fail. Which feature of Delta Live Tables meets this requirement?
optionA: Error Handling
optionB: Change Data Capture
optionC: Monitoring
optionD: Expectations
explanation:
Expectations are the Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines (formerly Delta Live Tables) feature for data quality. An expectation is a constraint plus an action taken when a record violates it, and the documented actions are: warn (EXPECT, the default) writes invalid records to the target; drop (EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW) removes them before the write and logs the dropped count alongside other dataset metrics; fail (EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE) stops the update entirely.
This question asks for the sensor readings outside expected parameters to be dropped while the stream keeps running, which is exactly ON VIOLATION DROP ROW. Error Handling is not a named Delta Live Tables feature; Change Data Capture propagates row changes into a target and does nothing about validity; Monitoring reports on a pipeline after the fact rather than filtering records inside it.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

The two scraped snapshots of this item disagreed: the v2026-06-09 copy keys Expectations and the v2026-07-28 copy keyed Error Handling. The documentation settles it for Expectations.

question: A data engineer works for an organization that must meet a stringent Service Level Agreement (SLA) that demands minimal runtime errors and high availability for its data processing pipelines. The data engineer wants to avoid the operational overhead of managing and tuning clusters. Which architectural solution will meet the requirements?
optionA: Deploy a dedicated, manually managed cluster optimized by in-house IT staff.
optionB: Utilize Databricks serverless compute that automatically optimizes resources and abstracts cluster management.
optionC: Use an auto-scaling cluster configured and monitored by the user.
optionD: Implement a hybrid approach with scheduled batch jobs on custom cloud VMs.
explanation:
Serverless compute is the option that removes cluster management entirely. Databricks provisions the capacity, sizes and scales it, applies runtime upgrades and replaces unhealthy instances, so the team gets high availability and consistent performance without anyone tuning a cluster.
The other three all keep the operational burden the question is trying to shed. A dedicated manually managed cluster puts sizing and patching back on in-house staff; an auto-scaling cluster still has to be configured and monitored by the user, and autoscaling only varies the worker count within bounds someone chose; and scheduled jobs on custom cloud VMs abandons the platform's management entirely, which is the most operational overhead of the four, not the least.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/

question: What is the maximum output supported by a job cluster to ensure a notebook does not fail?
optionA: 30MBS
optionB: 25MBS
optionC: 15MBS
optionD: 10MBS
explanation:
Databricks documents the job cluster notebook output ceiling as 30 MB: "Job clusters have a maximum notebook output size of 30 MB." Exceeding it is what fails the notebook, which is what this question asks about.
The 10 MB figure is a different limit and is a default rather than a ceiling: "The maximum cell output size defaults to 10 MB", adjustable per notebook between 1 MB and 20 MB with the %set_cell_max_output_size_in_mb magic, or up to 20 MB on Databricks Runtime 12.2 and above via spark.databricks.driver.maxReplOutputLength. So 10 MB is a per-cell default, 20 MB is the per-cell maximum, and 30 MB is the job cluster output maximum the question is asking for.

question: A data engineer wants to create a new table containing the names of customers that live in France. They have written the following command: A senior data engineer mentions that it is organization policy to include a table property indicating that the new table includes personally identifiable information (PII). Which of the following lines of code fills in the above blank to successfully complete the task?
optionA: There is no way to indicate whether a table contains PII.
optionB: "COMMENT PII"
optionC: TBLPROPERTIES PII
optionD: COMMENT "Contains PII"
optionE: PII
explanation:
COMMENT "Contains PII" is the line that completes this statement. COMMENT takes a bare string literal in exactly this position, so it parses, and it attaches the PII marker to the table where anyone inspecting it will see it.
TBLPROPERTIES is a genuine way to tag a table, which is what makes it the tempting distractor, but it is not valid on its own. Its documented syntax takes parenthesised key-value pairs -- TBLPROPERTIES ( { property_key [ = ] property_val } [, ...] ), where the value must be a BOOLEAN, STRING, INTEGER or DECIMAL literal -- so a bare TBLPROPERTIES PII is a syntax error. Written properly it would be TBLPROPERTIES ('PII' = 'true'), which is not what that option offers.
Of the rest, "COMMENT PII" quotes the keyword itself rather than the message, a bare PII is not a clause at all, and the claim that a table cannot be marked for PII is simply false.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-tblproperties

question: Which of the following describes a benefit of creating an external table from Parquet rather than CSV when using a CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statement?
optionA: Parquet files can be partitioned
optionB: CREATE TABLE AS SELECT statements cannot be used on files
optionC: Parquet files have a well-defined schema
optionD: Parquet files have the ability to be optimized
optionE: Parquet files will become Delta tables
explanation:
Option C is the correct answer because Parquet files have a well-defined schema that is embedded within the data itself. This means that the data types and column names of the Parquet files are automatically detected and preserved when creating an external table from them. This also enables the use of SQL and other structured query languages to access and analyze the data. CSV files, on the other hand, do not have a schema embedded in them, and require specifying the schema explicitly or inferring it from the data when creating an external table from them. This can lead to errors or inconsistencies in the data types and column names, and also increase the processing time and complexity.

question:
A data engineer has been given a new record of data:
```
id STRING = 'a1'
rank INTEGER = 6
rating FLOAT = 9.4
```
Which of the following SQL commands can be used to append the new record to an existing Delta table my_table?
optionA:
```sql
INSERT INTO my_table VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
```
optionB:
```sql
my_table UNION VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
```
optionC:
```sql
INSERT VALUES ( 'a1' , 6, 9.4) INTO my_table
```
optionD:
```sql
UPDATE my_table VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4)
```
optionE:
```sql
UPDATE VALUES ('a1', 6, 9.4) my_table
```
explanation:
To append a new record to an existing Delta table, you can use the INSERT INTO statement with the VALUES clause. This statement will insert one or more rows into the table with the specified values.
Option A is the only code block that follows this syntax correctly. Option B is incorrect, as it uses the UNION operator, which will return a new table that is the union of two tables, not append to an existing table. Option C is incorrect, as it uses the INSERT VALUES statement, which is not a valid SQL syntax.
Option D is incorrect, as it uses the UPDATE statement, which will modify existing rows in the table, not append new rows. Option E is incorrect, as it uses the UPDATE VALUES statement, which is also not a valid SQL syntax. References: Insert data into a table using SQL | Databricks on AWS, Insert data into a table using SQL - Azure Databricks, Delta Lake Quickstart - Azure Databricks

question: What is the structure of an Asset Bundle?
optionA: A YAML configuration file that specifies the artifacts, resources, and configurations for the project.
optionB: A Docker image containing runtime environments and the source code of the assets
optionC: A single plain text file enumerating the names of assets to be migrated to a new workspace.
optionD: A compressed archive (ZIP) that solely contains workspace assets without any accompanying metadata.
explanation:
A Databricks Asset Bundle is defined in YAML. The bundle's configuration file -- databricks.yml at the project root -- declares the bundle name, its targets (such as dev and prod), workspace settings, permissions, and the resources the project deploys, which is how jobs and pipelines get expressed as code and version-controlled alongside the source they run.
The other options describe packaging formats that bundles do not use. A bundle is not a Docker image, is not a bare list of asset names, and is not a ZIP of workspace files -- the whole point is that the metadata travels with the project in readable, reviewable configuration.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/

question: A data engineer is attempting to write Python and SQL in the same command cell and is running into an error The engineer thought that it was possible to use a Python variable in a select statement. Why does the command fail?
optionA: Databricks supports language interoperability in the same cell but only between Scala and SQL
optionB: Databricks supports one language per cell.
optionC: Databricks supports multiple languages but only one per notebook.
optionD: Databricks supports language interoperability but only if a special character is used.
explanation:
A Databricks notebook cell runs in exactly one language. The notebook has a default language, and a cell either inherits it or overrides it wholesale, either by picking a language from the cell's language button or by putting a %python, %sql, %r or %scala magic at the very beginning of the cell. Either way the whole cell is then that one language, so Python and SQL cannot be interleaved inside a single command cell and the attempt fails.
The magic command is therefore not a way to mix two languages in one cell -- it changes which single language that cell uses. To pass a Python variable into SQL, keep them in separate cells and use spark.sql() with an f-string, or a widget, rather than trying to write both languages together.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/notebooks-code

The override applies to the entire cell, so the reason the command fails is one language per cell. question: Identify the impact of ON VIOLATION DROP ROW and ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE for a constraint violation. A data engineer has created an ETL pipeline using Delta Live table to manage their company travel reimbursement detail, they want to ensure that the if the location details has not been provided by the employee, the pipeline needs to be terminated. How can the scenario be implemented?
optionA:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location != NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL
```
optionB:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location != NULL) ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
```
optionC:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location = NULL)
```
optionD:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_location EXPECT (location != NULL) ON DROP ROW
```
explanation:
The requirement is that the pipeline stop when an employee has not supplied location details, and ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE is the expectation action documented for that: "Invalid records prevent the update from succeeding. Manual intervention is required before reprocessing." The alternatives do something else -- omitting the ON VIOLATION clause leaves the default warn behaviour, which writes the invalid record to the target and only records a metric, and ON VIOLATION DROP ROW discards the row while letting the pipeline continue. Neither terminates the pipeline.
Two caveats about this item as printed. The valid SQL for a null test is location IS NOT NULL; location != NULL evaluates to NULL for every row and so never fires. Option D's ON DROP ROW and option A's bare ON VIOLATION FAIL are not real syntax either -- the documented forms are ON VIOLATION DROP ROW and ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE. Option B is right on the clause the question is testing, which is what the exam is asking.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

corrected.note: Answer stands. The expectations table documents ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE as the action that prevents the update from succeeding. Flagging that every option in this item uses != NULL, which is not a working null test in SQL; the item tests the ON VIOLATION clause, not the predicate.

question: A data engineer is maintaining an ETL pipeline code with a GitHub repository linked to their Databricks account. The data engineer wants to deploy the ETL pipeline to production as a databricks workflow. Which approach should the data engineer use?
optionA: Manually create and manage the workflow in Ul
optionB: Maintain workflow_conf ig. json and deploy it using Terraform
optionC: Maintain workflow_config.j son and deploy it using Databricks CLI
optionD: Databricks Asset Bundles (DAB) + GitHub Integration
explanation:
Databricks Asset Bundles combined with the existing GitHub integration is the supported path from a Git-managed ETL repository to a production workflow. The job is declared in the bundle's YAML, lives in the same repository as the code it runs, and is deployed with the Databricks CLI -- which a GitHub Actions workflow can invoke, so promotion to production is a reviewable commit rather than a manual step.
Manually creating the workflow in the UI leaves production configuration undocumented and unreproducible. Hand-maintaining a workflow_config.json and deploying it with the CLI reinvents what bundles already standardise. Terraform can manage Databricks resources and is a legitimate tool for platform-level infrastructure, but for shipping a pipeline that already lives in a linked GitHub repo, bundles are the purpose-built answer.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/ci-cd

question: A data engineer has developed a data pipeline to ingest data from a JSON source using Auto Loader, but the engineer has not provided any type inference or schema hints in their pipeline. Upon reviewing the data, the data engineer has noticed that all of the columns in the target table are of the string type despite some of the fields only including float or boolean values. Which of the following describes why Auto Loader inferred all of the columns to be of the string type?
optionA: There was a type mismatch between the specific schema and the inferred schema
optionB: JSON data is a text-based format
optionC: Auto Loader only works with string data
optionD: All of the fields had at least one null value
optionE: Auto Loader cannot infer the schema of ingested data
explanation:
JSON data is a text-based format that represents data as a collection of name-value pairs. By default, when Auto Loader infers the schema of JSON data, it treats all columns as strings. This is because JSON data can have varying data types for the same column across different files or records, and Auto Loader does not attempt to reconcile these differences. For example, a column named "age" may have integer values in some files, but string values in others. To avoid data loss or errors, Auto Loader infers the column as a string type.
However, Auto Loader also provides an option to infer more precise column types based on the sample data.
This option is called cloudFiles.inferColumnTypes and it can be set to true or false. When set to true, Auto Loader tries to infer the exact data types of the columns, such as integers, floats, booleans, or nested structures. When set to false, Auto Loader infers all columns as strings. The default value of this option is false. References: Configure schema inference and evolution in Auto Loader, Schema inference with auto loader (non-DLT and DLT), Using and Abusing Auto Loader's Inferred Schema, Explicit path to data or a defined schema required for Auto loader.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/schema

question: Which of the following describes a scenario in which a data engineer will want to use a single-node cluster?
optionA: When they are working interactively with a small amount of data
optionB: When they are running automated reports to be refreshed as quickly as possible
optionC: When they are working with SQL within Databricks SQL
optionD: When they are concerned about the ability to automatically scale with larger data
optionE: When they are manually running reports with a large amount of data
explanation:
The scenario in which a data engineer will want to use a single-node cluster is when they are working interactively with a small amount of data. A single-node cluster is a cluster consisting of an Apache Spark driver and no Spark workers1. A single-node cluster supports Spark jobs and all Spark data sources, including Delta Lake1. A single-node cluster is helpful for single-node machine learning workloads that use Spark to load and save data, and for lightweight exploratory data analysis1. A single-node cluster can run Spark locally, spawn one executor thread per logical core in the cluster, and save all log output in the driver log1. A single-node cluster can be created by selecting the Single Node button when configuring a cluster1.
The other options are not suitable for using a single-node cluster. When running automated reports to be refreshed as quickly as possible, a data engineer will want to use a multi-node cluster that can scale up and down automatically based on the workload demand2. When working with SQL within Databricks SQL, a data engineer will want to use a SQL Endpoint that can execute SQL queries on a serverless pool or an existing cluster3. When concerned about the ability to automatically scale with larger data, a data engineer will want to use a multi-node cluster that can leverage the Databricks Lakehouse Platform and the Delta Engine to handle large-scale data processing efficiently and reliably4. When manually running reports with a large amount of data, a data engineer will want to use a multi-node cluster that can distribute the computation across multiple workers and leverage the Spark UI to monitor the performance and troubleshoot the issues.

2: Autoscaling | Databricks on AWS
3: SQL Endpoints | Databricks on AWS
4: Databricks Lakehouse Platform | Databricks on AWS

question: A data engineer has a single-task Job that runs each morning before they begin working. After identifying an upstream data issue, they need to set up another task to run a new notebook prior to the original task. Which of the following approaches can the data engineer use to set up the new task?
optionA: They can clone the existing task in the existing Job and update it to run the new notebook.

explanation:
To set up the new task to run a new notebook prior to the original task in a single-task Job, the data engineer can use the following approach: In the existing Job, create a new task that corresponds to the new notebook that needs to be run. Set up the new task with the appropriate configuration, specifying the notebook to be executed and any necessary parameters or dependencies. Once the new task is created, designate it as a dependency of the original task in the Job configuration. This ensures that the new task is executed before the original task.

question: An organization plans to share a large dataset stored in a Databricks workspace on AWS with a partner organization whose Databricks workspace is hosted on Azure. The data engineer wants to minimize data transfer costs while ensuring secure and efficient data sharing. Which strategy will reduce data egress costs associated with cross-cloud data sharing?
optionA: Using Delta Sharing without any additional configurations
optionB: Configure VPN connection between AWS and Azure for faster data sharing
optionC: Sharing data via pre-signed URLs without monitoring egress costs
optionD: Migrating the dataset to Cloudflare R2 object storage before sharing
explanation:
Delta Sharing needs no additional configuration to keep cross-cloud transfer costs down, because it does not copy the dataset. The provider shares a table in place and the recipient reads the underlying files directly from the provider's cloud storage using short-lived signed URLs, so no second copy is created and nothing is staged in an intermediate location -- and the protocol works across clouds, which is exactly the AWS-to-Azure case here.
The alternatives all add cost or risk. A VPN between AWS and Azure is infrastructure to build and pay for, and does not remove egress. Hand-rolled pre-signed URLs discard the governance and auditing that Unity Catalog provides, and the option itself concedes egress goes unmonitored. Migrating to a different object store adds a full data movement before any sharing has happened.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/opensharing

question: A data engineer needs to determine whether to use the built-in Databricks Notebooks versioning or version their project using Databricks Repos. Which of the following is an advantage of using Databricks Repos over the Databricks Notebooks versioning?
optionA: Databricks Repos automatically saves development progress
optionB: Databricks Repos supports the use of multiple branches
optionC: Databricks Repos allows users to revert to previous versions of a notebook
optionD: Databricks Repos provides the ability to comment on specific changes
optionE: Databricks Repos is wholly housed within the Databricks Lakehouse Platform
explanation:
Databricks Repos is a visual Git client and API in Databricks that supports common Git operations such as cloning, committing, pushing, pulling, and branch management. Databricks Notebooks versioning is a legacy feature that allows users to link notebooks to GitHub repositories and perform basic Git operations. However, Databricks Notebooks versioning does not support the use of multiple branches for development work, which is an advantage of using Databricks Repos. With Databricks Repos, users can create and manage branches for different features, experiments, or bug fixes, and merge, rebase, or resolve conflicts between them. Databricks recommends using a separate branch for each notebook and following data science and engineering code development best practices using Git for version control, collaboration, and CI/CD. question: A data engineering team has noticed that their Databricks SQL queries are running too slowly when they are submitted to a non-running SQL endpoint. The data engineering team wants this issue to be resolved. Which of the following approaches can the team use to reduce the time it takes to return results in this scenario?
optionA: They can turn on the Serverless feature for the SQL endpoint and change the Spot Instance Policy to "Reliability Optimized."
optionB: They can turn on the Auto Stop feature for the SQL endpoint.
optionC: They can increase the cluster size of the SQL endpoint.
optionD: They can turn on the Serverless feature for the SQL endpoint.
optionE: They can increase the maximum bound of the SQL endpoint's scaling range
explanation:
Option D is the correct answer because it enables the Serverless feature for the SQL endpoint, which allows the endpoint to automatically scale up and down based on the query load. This way, the endpoint can handle more concurrent queries and reduce the time it takes to return results. The Serverless feature also reduces the cold start time of the endpoint, which is the time it takes to start the cluster when a query is submitted to a non- running endpoint. The Serverless feature is available for both AWS and Azure Databricks platforms.

question: Which of the following SQL keywords can be used to convert a table from a long format to a wide format?
optionA: PIVOT
optionB: CONVERT
optionC: WHERE
optionD: TRANSFORM
optionE: SUM
explanation:
The SQL keyword that can be used to convert a table from a long format to a wide format is PIVOT. The PIVOT clause is used to rotate the rows of a table into columns of a new table1. The PIVOT clause can aggregate the values of a column based on the distinct values of another column, and use those values as the column names of the new table1. The PIVOT clause can be useful for transforming data from a long format, where each row represents an observation with multiple attributes, to a wide format, where each row represents an observation with a single attribute and multiple values2. For example, the PIVOT clause can be used to convert a table that contains the sales of different products by different regions into a table that contains the sales of each product by each region as separate columns1.
The other options are not suitable for converting a table from a long format to a wide format. CONVERT is a function that can be used to change the data type of an expression3. WHERE is a clause that can be used to filter the rows of a table based on a condition4. TRANSFORM is a keyword that can be used to apply a user- defined function to a group of rows in a table5. SUM is a function that can be used to calculate the total of a numeric column.
1: PIVOT | Databricks on AWS
2: Reshaping Data - Long vs Wide Format | Databricks on AWS
3: CONVERT | Databricks on AWS
4: WHERE | Databricks on AWS
5: TRANSFORM | Databricks on AWS
[SUM | Databricks on AWS]

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-pivot

question: A data engineer manages multiple external tables linked to various data sources. The data engineer wants to manage these external tables efficiently and ensure that only the necessary permissions are granted to users for accessing specific external tables. How should the data engineer manage access to these external tables?
optionA: Use Unity Catalog to manage access controls and permissions for each external table individually.
optionB: Create a single user role with full access to all external tables and assign it to all users.
optionC: Grant permissions on the Databricks workspace level, which will automatically apply to all external tables.
optionD: Set up Azure Blob Storage permissions at the container level, allowing access to all external tables.
explanation:
Unity Catalog is the governance layer for external tables, and it grants privileges per securable object. The engineer can hold SELECT on one external table without holding it on the next, which is what "only the necessary permissions" requires, and the grants are enforced consistently across every workspace attached to the metastore.
The others all over-grant or bypass governance. A single role with full access to every external table is the opposite of least privilege. Workspace-level permissions do not express table-level access. Setting permissions on the storage container governs the files rather than the tables, which both loses per-table granularity and lets a user reach the data outside Databricks entirely, where Unity Catalog cannot audit it.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/

question: A data engineer has been using a Databricks SQL dashboard to monitor the cleanliness of the input data to a data analytics dashboard for a retail use case. The job has a Databricks SQL query that returns the number of store-level records where sales is equal to zero. The data engineer wants their entire team to be notified via a messaging webhook whenever this value is greater than 0. Which of the following approaches can the data engineer use to notify their entire team via a messaging webhook whenever the number of stores with $0 in sales is greater than zero?
optionA: They can set up an Alert with a custom template.
optionB: They can set up an Alert with a new email alert destination.
optionC: They can set up an Alert with one-time notifications.

optionE: They can set up an Alert without notifications.
explanation:

After that, the data engineer can create an alert for their Databricks SQL query, and select the webhook alert destination as the notification destination. The alert can also be configured with a recurrence interval, such as every hour, to check the query result periodically. When the alert condition is met, the data engineer and their team will receive a notification via the messaging webhook, with the custom message and a link to the Databricks SQL query. The other options are either not suitable for sending notifications via a messaging webhook (A, B, E), or not suitable for sending recurring notifications ©. question: Which of the following data lakehouse features results in improved data quality over a traditional data lake?
optionA: A data lakehouse provides storage solutions for structured and unstructured data.
optionB: A data lakehouse supports ACID-compliant transactions.

question:
A data engineer needs to create a table in Databricks using data from a CSV file at location /path/to/csv. They run the following command:
```sql
CREATE TABLE new_table
_____
OPTIONS (
  header = "true",
  delimiter = "|"
)
LOCATION "path/to/csv"
```
Which of the following lines of code fills in the above blank to successfully complete the task?
optionA: USING DELTA
optionB: FROM CSV
optionC: None of these lines of code are needed to successfully complete the task
optionD: FROM "path/to/csv"
optionE: USING CSV
explanation:
USING CSV completes the statement. In CREATE TABLE the USING clause names the file format the table is backed by, so USING CSV tells Databricks to read the files at the given location as CSV.
USING DELTA would declare the wrong format for a CSV source. FROM CSV and FROM "path/to/csv" borrow query syntax -- FROM belongs in a SELECT, not in a table definition, and the location is already supplied by the statement's LOCATION clause. And the clause is not optional here: without USING, the table would fall back to the default format rather than reading the CSV data as intended.

question: Which two components function in the DB platform architecture's control plane? (Choose two.)
optionA: Compute Orchestration
optionB: Unity Catalog
optionC: Virtual Machines
optionD: Compute
optionE: Serverless Compute
explanation:
Compute Orchestration and Unity Catalog both run in the control plane. The control plane holds the backend services Databricks manages in its own account -- the web application, the service that schedules and orchestrates compute, and the Unity Catalog metastore that governs data across workspaces.
The other three belong to the compute plane, which is where data is actually processed. Virtual machines and compute are the resources that run the workloads, sitting in the customer's cloud account for classic compute; serverless compute is the same processing role, just run in a Databricks-managed serverless compute plane instead. The dividing line is management versus processing, not who pays for it.

question: Which of the following must be specified when creating a new Delta Live Tables pipeline?
optionA: A key-value pair configuration
optionB: The preferred DBU/hour cost
optionC: A path to cloud storage location for the written data
optionD: A location of a target database for the written data
optionE: At least one notebook library to be executed
explanation:
Option E is the correct answer because it is the only mandatory requirement when creating a new Delta Live Tables pipeline. A pipeline is a data processing workflow that contains materialized views and streaming tables declared in Python or SQL source files. Delta Live Tables infers the dependencies between these tables and ensures updates occur in the correct order. To create a pipeline, you need to specify at least one notebook library to be executed, which contains the Delta Live Tables syntax. You can also specify multiple libraries of different languages within your pipeline. The other options are optional or not applicable for creating a pipeline. Option A is not required, but you can optionally provide a key-value pair configuration to customize the pipeline settings, such as the storage location, the target schema, the notifications, and the pipeline mode.
Option B is not applicable, as the DBU/hour cost is determined by the cluster configuration, not the pipeline creation. Option C is not required, but you can optionally specify a storage location for the output data from the pipeline. If you leave it empty, the system uses a default location. Option D is not required, but you can optionally specify a location of a target database for the written data, either in the Hive metastore or the Unity Catalog.

question: A data engineer needs to combine sales data from an on-premises PostgreSQL database with customer data in Azure Synapse for a comprehensive report. The goal is to avoid data duplication and ensure up-to-date information How should the data engineer achieve this using Databricks?
optionA: Export data from both sources to CSV files and upload them to Databricks
optionB: Develop custom ETL pipelines to ingest data into Databricks
optionC: Manually synchronize data from both sources into a single database
optionD: Use Lakehouse Federation to query both data sources directly
explanation:
Lakehouse Federation lets Databricks query the PostgreSQL and Synapse data where it already lives. A foreign catalog is registered for each source, its tables become queryable through Unity Catalog, and a single query can join across them -- so there is no copy to fall out of date and no duplication, which is precisely what the question asks for.
Every alternative moves the data. Exporting to CSV produces a snapshot that is stale the moment it is written. Custom ETL pipelines create and then have to maintain a second copy. Manual synchronisation is the same problem done by hand, with more room for drift.

question: A new data engineering team has been assigned to work on a project. The team will need access to database customers in order to see what tables already exist. The team has its own group team. Which of the following commands can be used to grant the necessary permission on the entire database to the new team?
explanation:
Seeing which tables exist in a database requires the privilege that lets a principal traverse into the containing object, and among these options only GRANT USAGE ON DATABASE customers TO team; does that. question: A departing platform owner currently holds ownership of multiple catalogs and controls storage credentials and external locations. The data engineer wants to ensure continuity: transfer catalog ownership to the platform team group, delegate ongoing privilege management, and retain the ability to receive and share data via Delta Sharing. Which role must be in place to perform these actions across the metastore?
optionA: Account Admin, because account admins can only create metastores but cannot change ownership of catalogs.
optionB: Workspace Admin, because workspace admins can transfer ownership of any Unity Catalog object.
optionC: Metastore Admin, because metastore admins can transfer ownership and manage privileges across all metastore objects, including shares and recipients.
optionD: Catalog Owner, because catalog owners can transfer any object in any catalog in the metastore.
explanation:
In Unity Catalog, the Metastore Admin role has the highest level of authority within a metastore and is responsible for governing all data assets registered in that metastore. Metastore admins can transfer ownership of catalogs, manage privileges across all securable objects (catalogs, schemas, tables, views), and administer storage credentials, external locations, and Delta Sharing objects such as shares and recipients.
This makes the role essential when a platform owner departs and continuity must be maintained at an organizational level. Workspace admins (option B) manage workspace-level settings but do not automatically have authority over Unity Catalog ownership unless explicitly granted. Catalog owners (option D) are limited to a single catalog and cannot perform actions across the entire metastore. Account admins (option A) operate at the account level and are primarily responsible for creating metastores and assigning admins, not for day-to-day governance within an existing metastore. Databricks documentation clearly defines the Metastore Admin as the role required to centrally manage ownership, privileges, and data sharing across the metastore in Databricks.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/manage-privileges/admin-privileges

question: In which of the following scenarios should a data engineer use the MERGE INTO command instead of the INSERT INTO command?
optionA: When the location of the data needs to be changed
optionB: When the target table is an external table
optionC: When the source table can be deleted
optionD: When the target table cannot contain duplicate records
optionE: When the source is not a Delta table
explanation:
The MERGE INTO command is used to perform upserts, which are a combination of insertions and updates, based on a source table into a target Delta table1. The MERGE INTO command can handle scenarios where the target table cannot contain duplicate records, such as when there is a primary key or a unique constraint on the target table. The MERGE INTO command can match the source and target rows based on a merge condition and perform different actions depending on whether the rows are matched or not. For example, the MERGE INTO command can update the existing target rows with the new source values, insert the new source rows that do not exist in the target table, or delete the target rows that do not exist in the source table1.
The INSERT INTO command is used to append new rows to an existing table or create a new table from a query result2. The INSERT INTO command does not perform any updates or deletions on the existing target table rows. The INSERT INTO command can handle scenarios where the location of the data needs to be changed, such as when the data needs to be moved from one table to another, or when the data needs to be partitioned by a certain column2. The INSERT INTO command can also handle scenarios where the target table is an external table, such as when the data is stored in an external storage system like Amazon S3 or Azure Blob Storage3. The INSERT INTO command can also handle scenarios where the source table can be deleted, such as when the source table is a temporary table or a view4. The INSERT INTO command can also handle scenarios where the source is not a Delta table, such as when the source is a Parquet, CSV, JSON, or Avro file5.
1: MERGE INTO | Databricks on AWS
2: [INSERT INTO | Databricks on AWS]
3: [External tables | Databricks on AWS]
4: [Temporary views | Databricks on AWS]
5: [Data sources | Databricks on AWS]
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/delta-merge-into

question: A data engineer has three tables in a Delta Live Tables (DLT) pipeline. They have configured the pipeline to drop invalid records at each table. question: A team creates YAML manifests that declare jobs, resources, and dependencies, then deploys them to Databricks using the Databricks CLI. The deployment succeeds. Which feature are they using?

question:
A data engineer has joined an existing project and they see the following query in the project repository:
```sql
CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE loyal_customers AS
SELECT customer_id
FROM STREAM(LIVE.customers)
WHERE loyalty_level = 'high';
```
Which of the following describes why the STREAM function is included in the query?
optionA: The STREAM function is not needed and will cause an error.
optionB: The table being created is a live table.
optionC: The customers table is a streaming live table.
optionD: The customers table is a reference to a Structured Streaming query on a PySpark DataFrame.
optionE: The data in the customers table has been updated since its last run.
explanation:
The STREAM function is used to process data from a streaming live table or view, which is a table or view that contains data that has been added only since the last pipeline update. Streaming live tables and views are stateful, meaning that they retain the state of the previous pipeline run and only process new data based on the current query. This is useful for incremental processing of streaming or batch data sources. The customers table in the query is a streaming live table, which means that it contains the latest data from the source. The STREAM function enables the query to read the data from the customers table incrementally and create another streaming live table named loyal_customers, which contains the customer IDs of the customers with high loyalty level. question: Identify how the count_if function and the count where x is null can be used Consider a table random_values with below data. What would be the output of below query? select count_if(col > 1) as count_a. count(*) as count_b.count(col1) as count_c from random_values col1 0 1 2 NULL - 2 3
explanation:
The result is 3, 6, 5, and each column is worth stepping through against the values 0, 1, 2, NULL, 2, 3.
count_if(col1 > 1) counts rows where the predicate is true: 2, 2 and 3 qualify, so 3. Note that the NULL row does not qualify -- NULL > 1 evaluates to NULL rather than true, so it is not counted.
count(*) counts rows regardless of content, including the NULL row, so 6.
count(col1) counts non-null values in that column, which excludes the NULL, so 5. That difference between count(*) and count(column) is the point of the question: the first counts rows, the second counts values.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/count_if

question: A data engineer is processing ingested streaming tables and needs to filter out NULL values in the order_datetime column from the raw streaming table orders_raw and store the results in a new table orders_valid using DLT. Which code snippet should the data engineer use?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_valid(
  CONSTRAINT valid_date
  EXPECT (order_datetime IS NOT NULL)
  ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
)
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM orders_raw;
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_valid
AS
SELECT *
FROM STREAM(orders_raw)
WHERE order_datetime IS NOT NULL
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE OR REFRESH STREAMING TABLE orders_valid
(
  CONSTRAINT valid_date EXPECT (order_datetime IS NOT NULL)
  ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
)
AS SELECT * FROM orders_raw;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE STREAMING TABLE orders_valid
(
  FILTER (order_datetime IS NOT NULL)
)
AS SELECT * FROM STREAM(orders_raw);
```
explanation:
Expectations are the documented Lakeflow Declarative Pipelines mechanism for filtering invalid records, and EXPECT ... ON VIOLATION DROP ROW is the action that drops violating rows before the write while logging the dropped count alongside other dataset metrics. Option A applies that constraint and reads the source as a stream, which is what a streaming table needs.
Option C declares the same constraint but reads AS SELECT * FROM orders_raw without STREAM, making it a batch read against a streaming source. Option D's FILTER (...) is not an expectations clause at all.
One caveat worth knowing: option B does technically produce the same rows, because a WHERE clause on a streaming read also removes the NULLs. It is not the mechanism this question is testing, and it discards the data-quality metrics that expectations record, but the item would be stronger if B were not also workable.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

The other scraped snapshot of this same question keys the expectations option, which agrees. Flagging that option B is also functionally valid, so this item has two workable answers and is weak.

question: A data engineer at a company that uses Databricks with Unity Catalog needs to share a collection of tables with an external partner who also uses a Databricks workspace enabled for Unity Catalog. The data engineer decides to use Delta Sharing to accomplish this. What is the first piece of information the data engineer should request from the external partner to set up Delta Sharing?
optionA: The IP address of their Databricks workspace
optionB: The sharing identifier of their Unity Catalog metastore
optionC: The name of their Databricks cluster
optionD: Their Databricks account password
explanation:
The first thing to request is the partner's sharing identifier for their Unity Catalog metastore. In Databricks-to-Databricks sharing the provider creates a recipient object, and that recipient is identified by the consumer's metastore sharing identifier -- a string of the form cloud:region:metastore-uuid. Without it the provider cannot create a recipient to share with, so it genuinely is the first piece of information needed.
The alternatives are either irrelevant or dangerous. A workspace IP address plays no part in Delta Sharing's identity model, and neither does a cluster name. A partner's account password should never be requested by anyone -- Delta Sharing is designed so that no credential ever changes hands.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/opensharing/share-data-databricks

question: A data engineering team has two tables. The first table march_transactions is a collection of all retail transactions in the month of March. The second table april_transactions is a collection of all retail transactions in the month of April. There are no duplicate records between the tables. Which of the following commands should be run to create a new table all_transactions that contains all records from march_transactions and april_transactions without duplicate records?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
INNER JOIN SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
UNION SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
OUTER JOIN SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
INTERSECT SELECT * from april_transactions;
```
optionE:
```sql
CREATE TABLE all_transactions AS
SELECT * FROM march_transactions
MERGE SELECT * FROM april_transactions;
```
explanation:
The correct command to create a new table that contains all records from two tables without duplicate records is to use the UNION operator. The UNION operator combines the results of two queries and removes any duplicate rows. The INNER JOIN, OUTER JOIN, and MERGE operators do not remove duplicate rows, and the INTERSECT operator only returns the rows that are common to both tables. question: An organization is looking for an optimized storage layer that supports ACID transactions and schema enforcement. Which technology should the organization use?
optionA: Delta Lake
optionB: Data lake
optionC: Unity Catalog
optionD: Cloud File Storage
explanation:
Delta Lake is the optimized storage layer that provides ACID transactions and schema enforcement. Databricks documents it as the default storage format for all tables: an open-source layer that adds a transaction log over files in the object store, which is what makes atomic commits and schema enforcement possible on data sitting in cloud storage.
A plain data lake is the thing Delta Lake improves on: raw files in object storage with no transaction log, so it offers neither ACID guarantees nor schema enforcement. Unity Catalog is the governance layer, handling access control and lineage rather than storage. Cloud file storage is the underlying object store the other layers sit on.

question: A data engineer streams customer orders into a Kafka topic (orders_topic) and is currently writing the ingestion script of a DLT pipeline. The data engineer needs to ingest the data from Kafka brokers to DLT using Databricks What is the correct code for ingesting the data?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE orders_raw
AS SELECT
    value:order_id AS order_id,
    value:customer_id AS customer_id,
    value:amount AS amount,
    value:order_status AS order_status,
    value:order_timestamp AS order_timestamp
FROM cloud_files("kafka://broker:9092/orders_topic", "json");
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE LIVE TABLE orders_raw
AS SELECT
    CAST(value AS STRING) AS json_data
FROM STREAM kafka.`broker:9092/orders_topic`;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE LIVE TABLE orders_raw
AS SELECT
    CAST(value AS STRING) AS json_data
FROM STREAM kafka.`broker:9092/orders_topic`;
```
explanation:

The keyed option imports dlt, decorates the function with @dlt.table, and returns spark.readStream.format("kafka") configured with kafka.bootstrap.servers, subscribe and startingOffsets -- the standard Kafka reader, wrapped so the pipeline manages the resulting table.
The SQL options fail for different reasons. One reads with cloud_files(), which is Auto Loader and only reads files from object storage, not a Kafka broker. The other declares CREATE LIVE TABLE, a materialised view recomputed from its source, when a continuously arriving Kafka topic needs a streaming table.
A defect worth knowing about this item: two of its four options are the same text, so it presents three distinct choices rather than four.

question: A data engineer has a Job with multiple tasks that runs nightly. Each of the tasks runs slowly because the clusters take a long time to start. Which of the following actions can the data engineer perform to improve the start up time for the clusters used for the Job?
optionA: They can use endpoints available in Databricks SQL
optionB: They can use jobs clusters instead of all-purpose clusters
optionC: They can configure the clusters to be single-node
optionD: They can use clusters that are from a cluster pool
optionE: They can configure the clusters to autoscale for larger data sizes
explanation:
The best action that the data engineer can perform to improve the start up time for the clusters used for the Job is to use clusters that are from a cluster pool. A cluster pool is a set of idle clusters that can be used by jobs or interactive sessions. By using a cluster pool, the data engineer can avoid the cluster creation time and reduce the latency of the tasks. Cluster pools also offer cost savings and resource efficiency, as they can be shared by multiple users and jobs.
Option A is not relevant, as endpoints available in Databricks SQL are used for creating and managing SQL analytics workloads, not for improving cluster start up time.
Option B is not correct, as jobs clusters and all-purpose clusters have similar start up times. Jobs clusters are clusters that are dedicated to run a single job and are terminated when the job is completed. All-purpose clusters are clusters that can be used for multiple purposes, such as interactive sessions, notebooks, or multiple jobs. Both types of clusters can benefit from using a cluster pool.
Option C is not advisable, as configuring the clusters to be single-node will reduce the parallelism and performance of the tasks. Single-node clusters are clusters that have only one worker node and are typically used for testing or development purposes. They are not suitable for running production jobs that require high scalability and fault tolerance.
Option E is not helpful, as configuring the clusters to autoscale for larger data sizes will not affect the start up time of the clusters. Autoscaling is a feature that allows clusters to dynamically adjust the number of worker nodes based on the workload. It can help optimize the resource utilization and cost efficiency of the clusters, but it does not speed up the cluster creation process.

question: A data engineer is writing a script that is meant to ingest new data from cloud storage. In the event of the Schema change, the ingestion should fail. It should fail until the changes downstream source can be found and verified as intended changes. Which command will meet the requirements?
optionA: addNewColumns
optionB: none
optionC: failOnNewColumns
optionD: rescue
explanation:
failOnNewColumns is the schema-evolution mode that stops and stays stopped. Databricks documents it as failing the stream and not restarting unless you update the provided schema or remove the offending file, which is exactly the requirement here: halt on a schema change and keep halting until a human has confirmed the upstream change was intended.
The default, addNewColumns, is the close distractor -- it also fails the stream, but it adds the new columns to the schema first, so restarting simply resumes with the changed schema and the unverified change flows through. rescue never fails at all; it routes unexpected columns into the rescued data column. And none silently ignores new columns, which is the worst outcome for a pipeline that is supposed to catch this.

question: Which of the following describes when to use the CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE (formerly CREATE INCREMENTAL LIVE TABLE) syntax over the CREATE LIVE TABLE syntax when creating Delta Live Tables (DLT) tables using SQL?
optionA: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when the subsequent step in the DLT pipeline is static.
optionB: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when data needs to be processed incrementally.
optionC: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE is redundant for DLT and it does not need to be used.
optionD: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when data needs to be processed through complicated aggregations.
optionE: CREATE STREAMING LIVE TABLE should be used when the previous step in the DLT pipeline is static.
explanation:
A streaming live table or view processes data that has been added only since the last pipeline update.
Streaming tables and views are stateful; if the defining query changes, new data will be processed based on the new query and existing data is not recomputed. This is useful when data needs to be processed incrementally, such as when ingesting streaming data sources or performing incremental loads from batch data sources. A live table or view, on the other hand, may be entirely computed when possible to optimize computation resources and time. This is suitable when data needs to be processed in full, such as when performing complex transformations or aggregations that require scanning all the data. References: Difference between LIVE TABLE and STREAMING LIVE TABLE, CREATE STREAMING TABLE, Load data using streaming tables in Databricks SQL.

question: A new data engineering team team has been assigned to an ELT project. The new data engineering team will need full privileges on the table sales to fully manage the project. question: A data engineer is inspecting an ETL pipeline based on a Pyspark job that consistently encounters performance bottlenecks. Based on developer feedback, the data engineer assumes the job is low on compute resources. To pinpoint the issue, the data engineer observes the Spark Ul and finds out the job has a high CPU time vs Task time. Which course of action should the data engineer take?
optionA: High CPU time vs Task time means an under-utilized cluster. The data engineer may need to repartition data to spread the jobs more evenly throughout the cluster.
optionB: High CPU time vs Task time means over-utilized memory and the need to increase parallelism
optionC: High CPU time vs Task time means a CPU over-utilized job. The data engineer may need to consider executor and core tuning or resizing the cluster
optionD: High CPU time vs Task time means efficient use of cluster and no change needed
explanation:
Task time is how long a task took end to end; CPU time is how much of that the executor spent actually computing. When CPU time accounts for most of task time, the cores are busy rather than idle, so the stage is compute-bound and the remedy is more or faster CPU: tune the executor and core counts, or move to a larger or Photon-enabled cluster.
The inverse reading is what makes the distractors wrong. A cluster that is under-utilized shows CPU time far below task time, because the tasks are waiting on I/O, shuffle or skew rather than computing; repartitioning helps that case, not this one. Memory pressure shows up as spill and GC time, not as elevated CPU time. And a high ratio is not by itself proof of an efficient job, since a slow UDF or an exploding join will burn CPU productively-looking but pointlessly.
A caveat on this item: Databricks documents cluster CPU utilization as a metric and publishes a Spark UI diagnosis guide, but it does not publish this specific CPU-time-versus-task-time rule of thumb. The reasoning above follows from what the two metrics measure rather than from a documented Databricks statement.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/cluster-metrics
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/spark-ui-guide/

corrected.note: Answer stands as the best-supported option, but flagging that Databricks does not document this heuristic. Its Spark UI guide diagnoses slow stages by I/O, small files, skew, spill and slow UDFs, and never frames a CPU-time to task-time ratio. Treat this item as reasoning from metric definitions, not from vendor guidance.

question: A single Job runs two notebooks as two separate tasks. A data engineer has noticed that one of the notebooks is running slowly in the Job's current run. The data engineer asks a tech lead for help in identifying why this might be the case. Which of the following approaches can the tech lead use to identify why the notebook is running slowly as part of the Job?
optionA: They can navigate to the Tasks tab in the Jobs UI to immediately review the processing notebook.
optionB: They can navigate to the Runs tab in the Jobs UI to immediately review the processing notebook.
optionC: There is no way to determine why a Job task is running slowly.
optionD: They can navigate to the Tasks tab in the Jobs UI and click on the active run to review the processing notebook.
optionE: They can navigate to the Runs tab in the Jobs UI and click on the active run to review the processing notebook.
explanation:
Job run details live under the Runs tab, and the run has to be opened before the notebook output is visible. Navigating to Runs and clicking into the active run reaches the task's output, its Spark UI and its logs, which is what diagnosing a slow notebook requires.
The Tasks tab shows how the job is defined -- its tasks, their dependencies and their settings -- not what any particular execution is doing, so it cannot explain a slow run in progress. The options that stop at a tab without opening a run skip the step where the diagnostic detail actually appears.

question: Which method should a Data Engineer apply to ensure Workflows are being triggered on schedule?
optionA: Scheduled Workflows can reduce resource consumption and expense since the cluster runs only long enough to execute the pipeline.
optionB: Scheduled Workflows run continuously until manually stopped.
optionC: Scheduled Workflows require an always-running cluster, which is more expensive but reduces processing latency.
optionD: Scheduled Workflows process data as it arrives at configured sources.
explanation:
Scheduling a workflow lets Databricks run it on job compute that is created for the run and terminated when it finishes, so the cluster exists only for as long as the pipeline takes. That is why a scheduled workflow reduces both resource consumption and cost compared with leaving compute available around the clock.
The other statements misdescribe how schedules behave. A scheduled workflow does not run continuously until stopped -- it starts at its trigger time and ends when the run completes. It does not require an always-running cluster; that describes an all-purpose cluster left on. And processing data as it arrives describes file-arrival or continuous triggering, which is a different trigger type from a schedule.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/triggers

question: A data engineer is getting a partner organization up to speed with Databricks account. Both teams share some business use cases. The data engineer has to share some of your Unity-Catalog managed delta tables and the notebook jobs creating those tables with the partner organization. How can the data engineer seamlessly share the required information?
optionA: Zip all the code and share via email and allow data ingestion from your data lake
optionB: Data and Notebooks can be shared simply using Unity Catalog.
optionC: Share required datasets and notebooks via Delta Sharing. Manage permissions via Unity Catalog.
optionD: Share access to codebase via Github and allow them to ingest datasets from your Datalake.
explanation:
Delta Sharing is what moves the data across organisational boundaries, and Unity Catalog is what governs who may see it. The provider creates a share containing the required tables, and Databricks-to-Databricks sharing can carry notebook files alongside them, so the partner receives both the datasets and the notebooks that build them without either side copying anything.
The distractor worth taking seriously is the one naming Unity Catalog alone. Unity Catalog governs objects within a metastore; it does not by itself hand data to a different organisation's account. Sharing is the transport, Unity Catalog is the permission model, and the question needs both. Zipping code into an email or handing over a GitHub repository shares the code but leaves the data access ungoverned and unaudited.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/opensharing/share-data-databricks

question: A data engineer and data analyst are working together on a data pipeline. The data engineer is working on the raw, bronze, and silver layers of the pipeline using Python, and the data analyst is working on the gold layer of the pipeline using SQL The raw source of the pipeline is a streaming input. Delta Live Tables support multi-language pipelines, allowing data engineers and data analysts to work in their preferred languages, such as Python for data engineering tasks (raw, bronze, and silver layers) and SQL for data analytics tasks (gold layer). This capability is particularly beneficial in collaborative settings and leverages the strengths of each language for different stages of data processing.

question: A data engineer has been using a Databricks SQL dashboard to monitor the cleanliness of the input data to an ELT job. The ELT job has its Databricks SQL query that returns the number of input records containing unexpected NULL values. The data engineer wants their entire team to be notified via a messaging webhook whenever this value reaches 100. Which of the following approaches can the data engineer use to notify their entire team via a messaging webhook whenever the number of NULL values reaches 100?

question: A data engineer needs to process SQL queries on a large dataset with fluctuating workloads. The workload requires automatic scaling based on the volume of queries, without the need to manage or provision infrastructure. The solution should be cost-efficient and charge only for the compute resources used during query execution. Which compute option should the data engineer use?
optionA: Databricks Jobs
optionB: Serverless SQL Warehouse
optionC: Databricks Runtime for ML
optionD: Databricks SQL Analytics
explanation:
A serverless SQL warehouse starts in seconds, scales up and back down with query volume, and bills only for the time it spends executing, which matches every constraint in the question -- fluctuating demand, no infrastructure to provision, and payment tied to actual use.
Databricks Jobs is an orchestrator rather than a SQL query engine; it schedules work, it does not answer interactive SQL. Databricks Runtime for ML is a runtime image aimed at model training, not a compute type for SQL analytics. question: What is stored in a Databricks customer's cloud account?

question: A data engineer is maintaining a data pipeline. Upon data ingestion, the data engineer notices that the source data is starting to have a lower level of quality. The data engineer would like to automate the process of monitoring the quality level. Which of the following tools can the data engineer use to solve this problem?
optionA: Unity Catalog
optionB: Auto Loader
optionC: Delta Live Tables
optionD: Delta Lake
optionE: Data Explorer
explanation:
Automating data-quality monitoring is what pipeline expectations are for. Declaring a constraint on a dataset makes each run evaluate incoming records against it and record how many passed and failed, so quality is tracked continuously as part of the pipeline instead of being spot-checked by hand -- and the action attached to the constraint decides whether violating rows are kept, dropped or made to fail the update.
The other tools each solve a neighbouring problem. Auto Loader ingests new files but does not judge their quality. Delta Lake enforces schema and gives ACID guarantees, which stops malformed writes but does not measure quality over time. Unity Catalog governs access. Catalog Explorer, listed here under its former name Data Explorer, is for browsing objects.

question: What are the transformations typically included in building the Bronze layer?
optionA: Include columns Load date/time, process ID
optionB: Business rules and transformations
optionC: Perform extensive data cleansing
optionD: Aggregate data from multiple sources
explanation:
The Bronze layer stores source data essentially as it arrived, so the only transformations belonging there are the ones that record provenance rather than change meaning: load date/time, a process or batch id, source file name. Those columns are what make a load auditable and reprocessable later.
Everything else listed belongs downstream. Extensive cleansing and standardisation is Silver's job, applying business rules is Silver-to-Gold work, and aggregating across sources is characteristic of Gold. Doing any of them at Bronze destroys the property that makes the layer useful -- that you can always go back to what the source actually sent.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer is decommissioning a sandbox schema in Unity Catalog. Some tables are ephemeral staging outputs that can be safety removed entirely, but a few tables point at shared cloud storage used by downstream jobs outside Databricks. The engineer must avoid deleting any shared files when cleaning up catalog objects. How does Unity Catalog behave when dropping Managed vs External tables?
optionA: DROP all tables; Databricks will only remove metadata for both managed and external tables.
optionB: DROP managed tables that are ephemeral and DROP external tables; files for both remain for 7 days.
optionC: DROP managed staging tables to remove data and metadata, and DROP external tables to remove only metadata
optionD: DROP external tables first to delete their files, then DROP managed tables to keep their files for recovery.

In Unity Catalog, dropping a managed table deletes both the table metadata and the underlying data files, while dropping an external table removes only the catalog metadata and leaves the referenced cloud storage data intact.

question: A data engineer is writing Spark code to group sales data by region and calculate total revenue for each region. Which Spark DataFrame transformation performs grouping operations?
optionA: orderBy
optionB: groupBy
optionC: filter
optionD: select
explanation:
groupBy is the grouping transformation. It partitions rows by the values of the given column and returns a grouped object that an aggregation such as sum then reduces, producing one row per region.
The others operate on rows or columns without grouping anything: orderBy sorts, filter removes rows that fail a predicate, and select projects a subset of columns. Any of them can appear in the same pipeline, but none of them is what turns many rows per region into one.

question: A data engineer has realized that they made a mistake when making a daily update to a table. They need to use Delta time travel to restore the table to a version that is 3 days old. However, when the data engineer attempts to time travel to the older version, they are unable to restore the data because the data files have been deleted. Which of the following explains why the data files are no longer present?
optionA: The VACUUM command was run on the table
optionB: The TIME TRAVEL command was run on the table
optionC: The DELETE HISTORY command was run on the table

explanation:

When you run VACUUM with certain retention settings, it can delete older data files, which might include versions of data that are older than the specified retention period. If the data engineer is unable to restore the table to a version that is 3 days old because the data files have been deleted, it's likely because the VACUUM command was run on the table, removing the older data files as part of data cleanup.

question: A data engineer has configured a Structured Streaming job to read from a table, manipulate the data, and then perform a streaming write into a new table. The code block used by the data engineer is below: If the data engineer only wants the query to execute a micro-batch to process data every 5 seconds, which of the following lines of code should the data engineer use to fill in the blank?
optionA: trigger(continuous="5 seconds")
optionB: trigger("5 seconds")
optionC: trigger(processingTime="5 seconds")
optionD: trigger(once="5 seconds")
optionE: trigger()
explanation:
trigger(processingTime="5 seconds") sets a fixed micro-batch interval, which is exactly what the question describes -- run a micro-batch, wait until five seconds have elapsed, run the next.
The distractors each name a different trigger mode or a syntax that does not exist. trigger(continuous="5 seconds") selects continuous processing, an experimental Spark mode Databricks does not support, and the interval there is a checkpointing interval rather than a batch interval. trigger(once=...) takes a boolean and runs a single batch, not a repeating one. A bare trigger() and a bare trigger("5 seconds") are not valid calls -- the mode has to be named with a keyword argument.
