question: In which of the following scenarios should a data engineer select a Task in the Depends On field of a new Databricks Job Task?
optionA: When another task needs to fail before the new task begins
optionB: When another task needs to be replaced by the new task
optionC: When another task needs to use as little compute resources as possible
optionD: When another task has the same dependency libraries as the new task
optionE: When another task needs to successfully complete before the new task begins
explanation:
Depends on expresses task ordering: the new task waits until the named task has finished successfully before it starts. That is the whole meaning of the field, and it is what lets a job express a pipeline rather than a set of unrelated tasks.
The alternatives describe things the field does not do. It is not a failure trigger -- a dependency that fails leaves the dependent task unrun rather than starting it. It does not replace a task, does not influence how much compute anything uses, and does not relate to shared libraries, which are configured per task independently of ordering.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/configure-task

question: A data engineer needs to apply custom logic to identify employees with more than 5 years of experience in array column employees in table stores. The custom logic should create a new column exp_employees that is an array of all of the employees with more than 5 years of experience for each row. In order to apply this custom logic at scale, the data engineer wants to use the FILTER higher-order function. Which of the following code blocks successfully completes this task?
optionA:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (employees, years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionB:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    CASE WHEN employees.years_exp > 5 THEN employees
        ELSE NULL
    END AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionC:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (employees, i -> i.years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionD:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (exp_employees, i -> i.years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
optionE:
```sql
SELECT
    store_id,
    employees,
    FILTER (exp_employees, years_exp > 5) AS exp_employees
FROM stores;
```
explanation:
FILTER is a higher-order function, so its second argument has to be a lambda that names the element being tested: FILTER(employees, i -> i.years_exp > 5). The lambda runs per element of the array and keeps the ones satisfying the predicate, producing a new array per row -- which is what the question asks for.
Two distractors drop the lambda and write years_exp > 5 directly, which has no element to bind to and does not resolve. Two others filter exp_employees, the column being created, rather than employees, the column that exists. The CASE WHEN option is wrong in a subtler way: it tests employees.years_exp as though the column were a struct, and it returns the whole array or NULL rather than filtering element by element.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/filter

question: A Databricks workflow fails at the last stage due to an error in a notebook. This workflow runs daily. The data engineer fixes the mistake and wants to rerun the pipeline. This workflow is very costly and time-intensive to run. Which action should the data engineer do in order to minimise downtime and cost?
optionA: Re-run the entire workflow
optionB: Repair run
optionC: Restart the cluster
optionD: Switch to another cluster
explanation:
Repair run re-executes only the tasks that failed, together with anything downstream that never got to run, and reuses the successful output of everything before them. On an expensive, long pipeline whose last stage broke, that is the difference between rerunning one task and rerunning the whole thing.
Re-running the entire workflow produces the right result but repeats hours of work that already succeeded, which is exactly the cost the question asks to avoid. Restarting or switching the cluster addresses compute, and the failure here came from a mistake in the notebook -- new compute would run the same broken code.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/repair-job-failures

question: A data engineer is designing a streaming pipeline and wants to limit how long Spark maintains state information for aggregation queries. Which Structured Streaming feature defines how long late data can be processed?
optionA: Watermark
optionB: Cache
optionC: Checkpoint
optionD: Partition
explanation:
A watermark is how a streaming query bounds its state. It declares how late an event may arrive and still be counted, which lets Spark decide when a window can be finalised and its state discarded -- so it answers both halves of the question, how long late data is accepted and how long state is retained.
Checkpointing is the closest distractor and does something different: it records stream progress so a query can restart without reprocessing or losing data. It persists state rather than bounding it. Caching keeps data in memory for reuse and partitioning controls data layout; neither has anything to do with event-time lateness.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/watermarks

question: An engineering manager uses a Databricks SQL query to monitor ingestion latency for each data source. The manager checks the results of the query every day, but they are manually rerunning the query each day and waiting for the results. Which of the following approaches can the manager use to ensure the results of the query are updated each day?
optionA: They can schedule the query to refresh every 1 day from the SQL endpoint's page in Databricks SQL.
optionB: They can schedule the query to refresh every 1 day from the query's page in Databricks SQL.
optionC: They can schedule the query to run every 1 day from the Jobs UI.
optionD: They can schedule the query to refresh every 12 hours from the SQL endpoint's page in Databricks SQL.
optionE: They can schedule the query to run every 12 hours from the Jobs UI.
explanation:
A Databricks SQL query is scheduled from its own page. Opening the query and setting a refresh schedule there makes it re-run on that cadence and update its results -- and anything reading those results, such as a dashboard, picks up the refreshed output.
The options pointing at the SQL warehouse's page are looking in the wrong place: a warehouse is compute and has settings for size, scaling and auto-stop, but schedules belong to queries, not to the warehouse that runs them. The twelve-hour variants also answer a different question -- the manager checks the results once a day, so a daily refresh is what is asked for.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/user/queries/schedule-query

question:
A dataset has been defined using Delta Live Tables and includes an expectations clause:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > '2020-01-01') ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE
```
What is the expected behavior when a batch of data containing data that violates these constraints is processed?
optionA: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionB: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and flagged as invalid in a field added to the target dataset.
optionC: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionD: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and loaded into a quarantine table.
optionE: Records that violate the expectation cause the job to fail.
explanation:
The constraint here carries ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE, and that action stops the pipeline. Databricks documents it as invalid records preventing the update from succeeding, with manual intervention required before reprocessing -- so a batch containing a timestamp at or before 2020-01-01 fails the run outright.
The other options describe the two actions this constraint did not use. Writing violating rows to the target while logging them is the default warn behaviour, which is what a bare EXPECT does. Dropping them and recording the count is ON VIOLATION DROP ROW. Routing them to a quarantine table is a pattern you build yourself with additional datasets; no ON VIOLATION action does it for you.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: A data engineer is attempting to drop a Spark SQL table my_table and runs the following command: DROP TABLE IF EXISTS my_table; After running this command, the engineer notices that the data files and metadata files have been deleted from the file system. Which of the following describes why all of these files were deleted?
optionA: The table was managed
optionB: The table did not have a location
optionC: The table's data was larger than 10 GB
optionD: The table's data was smaller than 10 GB
optionE: The table was external
explanation:
Dropping a managed table removes its data as well as its metadata, because Databricks owns the storage for managed tables and treats the table definition and the files beneath it as one lifecycle.
An external table behaves the opposite way, which is what makes it the tempting distractor: dropping one removes the catalog entry and leaves the files untouched, so it cannot explain data files disappearing. The remaining options invent a rule -- nothing about DROP TABLE depends on the size of the data, and a table without a location is simply a managed table, which is the answer already given.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/managed

question: Which of the following data workloads will utilize a Gold table as its source?
optionA: A job that cleans data by removing malformatted records
optionB: A job that queries aggregated data designed to feed into a dashboard
optionC: A job that aggregates uncleaned data to create standard summary statistics
optionD: A job that ingests raw data from a streaming source into the Lakehouse
optionE: A job that enriches data by parsing its timestamps into a human-readable format
explanation:
Gold tables are the refined, aggregated end of the medallion architecture, so the workload that reads from them is the one already consuming business-ready output -- a job querying aggregated data to feed a dashboard.
The others all sit upstream and would read from earlier layers. Removing malformatted records and parsing timestamps into readable form are Bronze-to-Silver cleaning steps. Ingesting raw streaming data lands in Bronze. Aggregating *uncleaned* data is the giveaway in the remaining option: it works on data that has not been through Silver yet, so its source is not Gold no matter that its output is aggregated.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: Differentiate between all-purpose clusters and jobs clusters. A data engineering team has created a python notebook to load data from cloud storage, this job has been tested and now needs to be scheduled in production. Which would be the best cluster to be used in this case?
optionA: Any Unity Catalog-enabled cluster
optionB: All purpose cluster
optionC: Jobs Cluster
optionD: Serverless SQL warehouse
explanation:
A jobs cluster is the right compute for scheduled production work. It is created when the run starts, sized by the job's configuration, and terminated when the run ends, so nothing is paid for between nightly runs and each run gets a clean, predictable environment.
An all-purpose cluster is designed for interactive development, stays available between uses and is billed at a higher rate, which makes it the expensive choice for scheduled work. A serverless SQL warehouse runs SQL, not a Python notebook. And "any Unity Catalog-enabled cluster" describes a governance property rather than a cluster type, so it does not answer the question being asked.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/compute

question: A data engineer needs to develop integration tests for an ETL process and deploy a version- controlled, packaged workflow into production using an external job scheduler. Which tool should the data engineer use for this job?
optionA: Databricks Connect
optionB: Databricks Asset Bundles
optionC: Databricks Command Line Interface
optionD: Databricks Software Development Kit
explanation:
Databricks Asset Bundles package a project's jobs, pipelines and settings as YAML that lives in the repository beside the code. That makes the workflow version-controlled and reviewable, gives integration tests a defined target to deploy against, and produces a deployment an external scheduler can invoke through the CLI.
The other three are components rather than the packaging mechanism. The CLI is the tool bundles are deployed *with*, so it is the closest answer but not the thing that provides versioned packaging. Databricks Connect runs local code against a remote cluster, useful while developing but not for deployment. The SDK is a programmatic client for the REST API.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/bundles/

question: A data engineer has a Delta table containing old data files that are no longer referenced after several update and delete operations. To remove these unused files and reclaim storage space, which Delta Lake command should be executed?
optionA: OPTIMIZE
optionB: VACUUM
optionC: DESCRIBE HISTORY
optionD: CACHE TABLE
explanation:
VACUUM is the command that deletes files. Updates and deletes on a Delta table write new files and leave the superseded ones in place so time travel keeps working; VACUUM removes those unreferenced files once they are older than the retention threshold, which is what reclaims the storage.
OPTIMIZE is the closest distractor and does something different -- it compacts many small files into fewer large ones to speed up reads, without removing history. DESCRIBE HISTORY only reports the table's version log. CACHE TABLE loads data into memory for faster access and changes nothing on disk.
One consequence worth remembering: because VACUUM removes the files older versions depend on, running it also limits how far back time travel can reach.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/operations/vacuum

question: A global retail company sells products across multiple categories (e.g., Electronics, Clothing) and regions (e.g., North, South, East, West). The sales team has provided the data engineer with a PySpark dataframe named sales_df as below and the team wants the data engineer to analyze the sales data to help them make strategic decisions. Calculate the total sales amount for each product category and store the results in a new dataframe called category_sales. What will generate the expected result of category_sales?
optionA: category_sales = sales_df.groupBy("category").agg(sum("sales_amount").alias("total_sales_amount"))
optionB: category_sales = sales_df.sum("sales_amount").groupBy("category").alias("total_sales_amount"))
optionC: category_sales = sales_df.agg(sum("sales_amount").groupBy("category").alias("total_sales_amount"))
optionD: category_sales = sales_df.groupBy("region").agg(sum("sales_amount").alias("total_sales_amount"))
explanation:
The correct approach is to group by the product category and then aggregate the sum of sales_amount, aliasing it as total_sales_amount. This produces the expected totals: 500 for Electronics and 900 for Clothing.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-groupby

question: Which of the following code blocks will remove the rows where the value in column age is greater than 25 from the existing Delta table my_table and save the updated table?
optionA: UPDATE my_table WHERE age <= 25;
optionB: UPDATE my_table WHERE age > 25;
optionC: DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age <= 25;
optionD: SELECT * FROM my_table WHERE age > 25;
optionE: DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age > 25;
explanation:
DELETE FROM my_table WHERE age > 25; removes the rows the question describes and, because Delta tables are transactional, the change is committed to the table itself -- there is no separate save step.
The predicate is where the distractors bite. DELETE FROM ... WHERE age <= 25 deletes precisely the rows meant to be kept. The UPDATE statements are wrong twice over: UPDATE modifies rows rather than removing them, and as written they carry no SET clause. SELECT only reads, returning the matching rows and leaving the table untouched.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/delta-delete-from

question: A data architect has determined that a table of the following format is necessary: Which of the following code blocks uses SQL DDL commands to create an empty Delta table in the above format regardless of whether a table already exists with this name?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE table_name (
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
)
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE table_name WITH COLUMNS (
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
) USING DELTA
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS table_name (
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
)
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE table_name AS
SELECT
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
USING DELTA
```
optionE:
```sql
CREATE TABLE table_name AS
SELECT
  employeeId STRING,
  startDate DATE,
  avgRating FLOAT
```
explanation:
CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE creates the table when it is absent and overwrites the definition when it is present, which is what "regardless of whether a table already exists" asks for. Listing the columns and their types produces the empty table in the required shape, and Delta is the default format so no USING clause is needed.
CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS is the trap: it succeeds either way, but when a table of that name already exists it silently leaves the old definition in place, so the schema may not be the one required. The CTAS options are wrong structurally -- AS SELECT builds a table from query results, and a SELECT list cannot carry column type declarations. WITH COLUMNS is not valid syntax.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using

question: A data engineer team has decided to implement a new data platform on Databricks and is currently deciding how to store each kind of data on each data layer. What is the appropriate layer and data pairing for medallion architecture?
optionA: Silver Layer - Raw data from deposit account application
optionB: Bronze Layer - Summary of cash deposit amount for each country and city
optionC: Silver Layer - Cleansed master customer data
optionD: Gold Layer - Deduplicated money transfer transaction
explanation:
In the Medallion architecture, the Silver layer holds cleansed and conformed data (such as master customer data), which has been cleaned, validated, and standardized after ingestion from the Bronze layer.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer must deliver a trustworthy customer 360 dataset in Databricks for data scientists and BI teams. The engineer plans to join deduplicated customer records with cleaned transaction data, enforce schema and data quality checks, and create a conformed "customer_transactions"view. Later, highly aggregated, domain-specific tables (for weekly spend and executive summaries) will be produced for dashboards. Where should the engineer build the conformed "customer_transactions" dataset, and where should the aggregated, report-ready tables reside?
optionA: Build both "customer_transactions" and aggregated, report-ready tables in Silver to keep the model simpler.
optionB: Build "customer_transactions" in Bronze and put the aggregated, report-ready tables in Silver.
optionC: Build "customer_transactions" in Gold and put the aggregated, report-ready tables in Silver.
optionD: Build "customer_transactions" in Silver and put the aggregated, report-ready tables in Gold.
explanation:
The conformed customer_transactions dataset belongs in Silver because it represents cleaned, deduplicated, and validated data that is suitable for broad analytical use. Aggregated, domain- specific, and report-ready tables are best placed in Gold, as this layer is designed for highly curated datasets optimized for BI, dashboards, and executive reporting.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer needs to apply custom logic to string column city in table stores for a specific use case. In order to apply this custom logic at scale, the data engineer wants to create a SQL user- defined function (UDF). Which of the following code blocks creates this SQL UDF?
optionA:
```sql
CREATE UDF combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionB:
```sql
CREATE UDF combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURNS STRING
CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionC:
```sql
CREATE UDF combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionD:
```sql
CREATE FUNCTION combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
optionE:
```sql
CREATE FUNCTION combine_nyc(city STRING)
RETURNS STRING
RETURN CASE
  WHEN city = "brooklyn" THEN "new york"
  ELSE city
END;
```
explanation:
A SQL UDF is created with CREATE FUNCTION, must declare its return type with RETURNS, and must produce its value with RETURN. Only one option has all three: CREATE FUNCTION combine_nyc(city STRING) RETURNS STRING RETURN CASE ... END;
The distractors each drop one piece. CREATE UDF is not a keyword in Databricks SQL, which rules out three of them immediately. Among the rest, one omits RETURNS STRING so the function has no declared type, and another declares the type but starts the body with CASE instead of RETURN CASE, leaving the function with no return statement.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-sql-function

question: An organization has data stored across multiple external systems, including MySQL, Amazon Redshift, and Google BigQuery. The data engineer wants to perform analytics without ingesting directly into Databricks, ensuring unified governance and minimizing data duplication. Which feature of Databricks enables querying these external data sources while maintaining centralized governance?
optionA: Delta Lake
optionB: Lakehouse Federation
optionC: MLflow
optionD: Databricks Connect
explanation:
Lakehouse Federation allows Databricks to query external data sources like MySQL, Redshift, and BigQuery without moving or duplicating data, while maintaining centralized governance through Unity Catalog.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/query-federation/

question:
A dataset has been defined using Delta Live Tables and includes an expectations clause:
```sql
CONSTRAINT valid_timestamp EXPECT (timestamp > '2020-01-01') ON VIOLATION DROP ROW
```
What is the expected behavior when a batch of data containing data that violates these constraints is processed?
optionA: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and flagged as invalid in a field added to the target dataset.
optionB: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and loaded into a quarantine table.
optionC: Records that violate the expectation are dropped from the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionD: Records that violate the expectation are added to the target dataset and recorded as invalid in the event log.
optionE: Records that violate the expectation cause the job to fail.
explanation:
This constraint carries ON VIOLATION DROP ROW, so violating records never reach the target. Databricks documents that action as dropping invalid records before the data is written, with the count of dropped records logged alongside the dataset's other metrics in the event log -- which is exactly what option C describes.
The alternatives belong to the other actions. Writing violating rows to the target and logging them is the default warn behaviour of a bare EXPECT. Failing the run is ON VIOLATION FAIL UPDATE. Quarantining into a separate table is a pattern you build with extra datasets rather than something an ON VIOLATION action does, and no action adds a validity flag column to the target.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: A Data Engineer is designing Bronze layer in Databricks Medallion Architecture. The raw data is collected from multiple sources (Clickstream in JSON, Transactions in CSV). The task is to design the Bronze layer of the Medallion Architecture to ingest and store this raw data for further processing. Which operation applies to the Bronze layer?
optionA: Ingest raw data without transformations, preserving original schemas, and store in Delta format.
optionB: Clean and standardize raw data by removing null values and enforcing schemas.
optionC: Apply complex business logic to enrich raw data with customer segmentation labels.
optionD: Aggregate and transform source data to calculate daily sales performance metrics.
explanation:
In the Bronze layer of the Medallion Architecture, raw data from multiple sources is ingested without transformations while preserving its original schema. The data is then stored in Delta format, serving as the single source of truth for downstream Silver and Gold layers where cleaning, standardization, and business logic are applied.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer has configured a Structured Streaming job to read from a table, manipulate the data, and then perform a streaming write into a new table. The code block used by the data engineer is below: The data engineer only wants the query to process all of the available data in as many batches as required. Which line of code should the data engineer use to fill in the blank?
optionA: trigger(continuous="once")
optionB: trigger(processingTime="once")
optionC: trigger(availableNow=True)
optionD: trigger(once=True)
explanation:
trigger(availableNow=True) is the option that processes everything currently available and then stops. Databricks describes it as consuming all available records as an incremental batch, with the batch size configurable through options such as maxBytesPerTrigger, which is exactly the "as many batches as required" behaviour the question asks for.
The near-miss is trigger(once=True): it also processes all available data and stops, but does so as a single batch, which can overwhelm a cluster when a large backlog has accumulated. It is also deprecated -- Databricks states that in Databricks Runtime 11.3 LTS and above, Trigger.Once is deprecated and recommends Trigger.AvailableNow for all incremental batch processing workloads. trigger(processingTime=...) runs on a fixed interval and never stops, and trigger(continuous=...) is an unsupported experimental Spark OSS feature.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/triggers

corrected.note: Answer stands. Added the specific distinction the item turns on -- AvailableNow splits the backlog into multiple incremental batches while Once uses a single batch -- and recorded that Trigger.Once has been deprecated since Databricks Runtime 11.3 LTS.

question: Which of the following commands will return the number of null values in the member_id column?
optionA: SELECT count(member_id) - count_null(member_id) FROM my_table;
optionB: SELECT null(member_id) FROM my_table;
optionC: SELECT count_if(member_id IS NULL) FROM my_table;
optionD: SELECT count(member_id) FROM my_table;
optionE: SELECT count_null(member_id) FROM my_table;
explanation:
count_if(member_id IS NULL) counts the rows where the predicate holds, so it returns the number of nulls directly. The IS NULL test matters: a comparison such as member_id = NULL would evaluate to NULL for every row and count nothing.
The other options rely on a function that does not exist -- there is no count_null in Databricks SQL, which rules out two of them. count(member_id) counts non-null values, so it gives the opposite number. A useful equivalent, if you want to remember only one form, is count(*) - count(member_id).
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/functions/count_if

question: What Databricks feature can be used to check the data sources and tables used in a workspace?
optionA: Use the lineage feature to visualize a graph that highlights where the table is used only in reports.
optionB: Use the lineage feature to visualize a graph that highlights where the table is used only in notebooks.
optionC: Use the lineage feature to visualize a graph that shows all dependencies, including where the table is used in notebooks, other tables, and reports.
optionD: Do not use the lineage feature as it only tracks activity from the last 3 months and will not provide full details on dependencies.
explanation:
Unity Catalog captures lineage automatically for queries run on Databricks, down to the column level, and aggregates it across every workspace attached to the metastore. The documentation describes it as showing which queries and files populate a table, which jobs and notebooks transform it, and which dashboards consume the results -- so the graph spans notebooks, downstream tables and reports together, not any one of them alone.
That also disposes of the retention objection. Lineage data displayed in Catalog Explorer is retained indefinitely, with all lineage captured after September 1, 2024 available; there is no three-month window.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/data-lineage

question: A data engineer is implementing a data ingestion pipeline that automatically detects schema changes in incoming JSON files and evolves the target Delta table accordingly. Which feature supports this automatic schema evolution?
optionA: Broadcast join
optionB: Partition pruning
optionC: Schema evolution
optionD: Schema enforcement
explanation:
Schema evolution is the feature that lets the target table's schema change as incoming data changes. In an Auto Loader pipeline it is controlled by cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode, whose default adds newly discovered columns to the schema; on the write side, the mergeSchema option lets a Delta write add new columns rather than reject them.
Schema enforcement is the deliberate opposite and is the tempting distractor: it rejects writes that do not match the current schema, protecting a table from unexpected columns rather than absorbing them. The two work together -- enforcement is the default guard, evolution is the explicit opt-in. Broadcast joins and partition pruning are query optimisations and have nothing to do with schema.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/schema
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/update-schema

question: A data engineer is setting up a new Databricks pipeline that ingests clickstream events from Kafka and daily product catalogs from cloud object storage. To ensure auditability and easy reprocessing, the engineer wants to land all source data. Later stages will handle cleaning, deduplication, and business modeling before the data is used in dashboards. Which approach aligns to Medallion Architecture principles?
optionA: Land both sources in Gold with denormalized star schemas to optimize BI while retaining full source fidelity.
optionB: Land streaming events from Kafka in silver, and the product catalog directly in Gold to minimize layers for batch data.
optionC: Land both sources in the Bronze layer append-only with minimal validation, then build Silver/Gold downstream for quality and analytics.
optionD: Land both sources directly into the Silver layer with schema enforcement and deduplication to reduce downstream complexity.
explanation:
The Medallion Architecture recommends landing all raw source data in the Bronze layer in an append-only, minimally transformed form to preserve source fidelity and support auditability and reprocessing, with cleaning, deduplication, and business modeling performed in downstream Silver and Gold layers.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineer wants to run SQL queries directly on data stored in Delta Lake using a serverless compute environment designed for analytics workloads. Which Databricks component provides this capability?
optionA: Spark Driver
optionB: DBFS
optionC: Databricks SQL Warehouse
optionD: MLflow
explanation:
A Databricks SQL warehouse is the compute built for running SQL against Delta Lake, and in its serverless form it starts in seconds, scales with demand and needs no infrastructure management -- which matches every part of the question.
The others are not query compute. The Spark driver is a component *inside* a cluster that coordinates work; it is not something you point SQL at. DBFS is a filesystem abstraction over object storage. MLflow tracks experiments and manages models.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/sql-warehouse/

question: A data engineer has a Python notebook in Databricks, but they need to use SQL to accomplish a specific task within a cell. They still want all of the other cells to use Python without making any changes to those cells. Which of the following describes how the data engineer can use SQL within a cell of their Python notebook?
optionA: They can simply write SQL syntax in the cell
optionB: They can attach the cell to a SQL endpoint rather than a Databricks cluster
optionC: It is not possible to use SQL in a Python notebook
optionD: They can change the default language of the notebook to SQL
optionE: They can add %sql to the first line of the cell
explanation:
Putting %sql on the first line of a cell switches that one cell to SQL while every other cell keeps the notebook's default language. That is precisely the requirement -- one cell changed, the rest untouched.
Writing bare SQL into a Python cell fails, because the cell is still interpreted as Python. Changing the notebook's default language to SQL would flip every cell, which the question rules out. Cells attach to the notebook's compute rather than being individually pointed at a SQL warehouse, so that option describes something that cannot be done per cell.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/notebooks-code

question: A data engineer wants to delete records from a Delta table where the status column equals "inactive". The operation should modify only the affected rows without rewriting the entire dataset. Which SQL command should be used?
optionA: DELETE
optionB: INSERT
optionC: MERGE
optionD: UPDATE
explanation:
DELETE removes the matching rows. On a Delta table it is a transactional operation that rewrites only the files containing rows that match the predicate, leaving every other file untouched -- which is the selective behaviour the question describes.
UPDATE modifies rows rather than removing them. INSERT adds rows. MERGE can delete as part of a conditional upsert against a source table, so it could technically be made to do this, but it is far more machinery than a single predicate needs and there is no source relation here to merge from.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/delta-delete-from

question: A data engineer wants to schedule multiple tasks in a workflow where each task depends on the successful completion of previous tasks. The workflow should support retries and monitoring. Which Databricks feature should be used?
optionA: DBFS
optionB: Databricks Jobs
optionC: Delta Lake
optionD: Spark UI
explanation:
Databricks Jobs is the orchestrator. A job holds multiple tasks, each task can declare the tasks it depends on so ordering is explicit, and the platform supplies retry policies, notifications and per-run monitoring -- every capability the question lists.
The others are not orchestration. DBFS is a filesystem abstraction, Delta Lake is the storage format, and the Spark UI is a diagnostic view of a single application's execution. Any of them may be involved in a pipeline, but none of them schedules or sequences work.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/

question:
A data engineer needs to create a table in Databricks using data from their organization's existing SQLite database. They run the following command:
```sql
CREATE TABLE jdbc_customer360
USING _____
OPTIONS (
  url "jdbc:sqlite:/customers.db",
  dbtable "customer360"
)
```
Which of the following lines of code fills in the above blank to successfully complete the task?
optionA: org.apache.spark.sql.jdbc
optionB: sqlite
optionC: autoloader
optionD: org.apache.spark.sql.sqlite
optionE: DELTA
explanation:
Reading an external relational database goes through Spark's JDBC data source, named org.apache.spark.sql.jdbc in the USING clause. The connection details -- the JDBC url, the driver class, and the table to read -- are then supplied through OPTIONS.
The distractors name formats that do not exist. There is no sqlite or org.apache.spark.sql.sqlite data source; SQLite is reached through JDBC like any other relational database, with the database-specific part living in the connection URL rather than in the format name. autoloader is not a USING format either, and DELTA would declare the table as Delta rather than reading from SQLite.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using

question: A data engineer wants to create an external table in Databricks that references data stored in an Azure Data Lake Storage (ADLS) location. The goal is to enable Databricks to access and query this external data without moving it into the Databricks-managed storage. Which step should the data engineer take to successfully create the external table?
optionA: Use the CREATE MANAGED TABLE statement and specify the LOCATION clause with the path to the external data.
optionB: CREATE UNMANAGED TABLE statement without specifying a LOCATION clause.
optionC: Use the CREATE TABLE statement and specify the LOCATION clause with the path to the external data.
optionD: CREATE EXTERNAL TABLE statement without specifying a LOCATION clause.
explanation:
To reference data stored outside of Databricks-managed storage, the engineer should use CREATE TABLE ... LOCATION 'path', which creates an unmanaged (external) table pointing to the ADLS data without moving it into Databricks storage.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/external

question: A data engineer notices that a Spark job performing a join between a large table and a small lookup table is slow. The lookup table is only a few megabytes. Which Spark optimization technique should be applied to improve the performance of the join operation?
optionA: Shuffle join
optionB: Broadcast join
optionC: Cartesian join
optionD: Sort merge join
explanation:
Broadcasting is the right optimisation when one side of a join is small. Spark sends a full copy of the small table to every executor so each one can join its partitions locally, which removes the shuffle of the large table entirely -- and at a few megabytes this lookup table is comfortably within broadcast range.
A shuffle or sort-merge join is what Spark falls back to for two large tables: both sides are repartitioned across the network by join key, which is the expensive behaviour being avoided here. A Cartesian join is not an optimisation at all; it pairs every row with every other row.
In practice adaptive query execution often selects a broadcast automatically once it sees the runtime size, but the join hint makes the intent explicit.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-qry-select-hints
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/aqe

question: A data engineer wants to create a data entity from a couple of tables. The data entity must be used by other data engineers in other sessions. It also must be saved to a physical location. Which of the following data entities should the data engineer create?
optionA: Table
optionB: Database
optionC: View
optionD: Function
optionE: Temporary view
explanation:
A table is the only entity here that both persists to a physical location and is visible to other users in other sessions. It is registered in the metastore, so anyone with the right privileges can query it later, and its data is written to storage rather than recomputed.
A view satisfies the sharing half but not the storage half: it is a saved query that materialises nothing, so it stores no data of its own. A temporary view fails both, disappearing when the session ends. A database is a container for tables rather than a data entity built from them, and a function encapsulates logic, not data.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/managed
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/views/

question: Which of the following describes the storage organization of a Delta table?
optionA: Delta tables are stored in a collection of files that contain data, history, metadata, and other attributes.
optionB: Delta tables store their data in a single file and all metadata in a collection of files in a separate location.
optionC: Delta tables are stored in a single file that contains data, history, metadata, and other attributes.
optionD: Delta tables are stored in a single file that contains only the data stored within the table.
optionE: Delta tables are stored in a collection of files that contain only the data stored within the table.
explanation:
A Delta table is a directory, not a file. The data lives in a collection of Parquet files, and beside them a _delta_log directory holds the transaction log -- JSON commits plus periodic checkpoints -- recording schema, metadata, statistics and the full version history.
That structure is what makes the rest of Delta work: time travel reads an earlier version from the log, ACID guarantees come from atomically appending a commit, and data skipping uses the per-file statistics stored there. Any option describing a single file is wrong, and so is any option describing only data files, since without the log there is no history, no metadata and no transactions.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/delta/

question: A data engineer needs to ingest streaming data from Kafka into a Delta Lake table using Databricks. The pipeline must guarantee exactly-once processing semantics and maintain checkpoint information to recover from failures. Which Spark Structured Streaming feature ensures reliable processing and fault tolerance?
optionA: Checkpointing
optionB: Watermarking
optionC: Caching
optionD: Partition pruning
explanation:
Checkpointing is what makes a streaming query recoverable. The checkpoint location stores the offsets processed in each batch along with the query's state, so after a failure the stream restarts from exactly where it stopped -- and combined with a replayable source such as Kafka and an idempotent sink such as Delta, that is what delivers exactly-once semantics.
Watermarking bounds how late an event may arrive and lets state be discarded; it governs correctness over event time rather than recovery. Caching keeps data in memory for reuse and partition pruning skips irrelevant files at read time; neither survives a restart or tracks progress.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/checkpoints

question: A Databricks single-task workflow fails at the last task due to an error in a notebook. The data engineer fixes the mistake in the notebook. What should the data engineer do to rerun the workflow?
optionA: Repair the task
optionB: Rerun the pipeline
optionC: Restart the cluster
optionD: Switch the cluster
explanation:
When a job run fails partway through, Databricks lets you repair that run rather than start a fresh one: a repair re-executes only the failed and skipped tasks, reusing the successful output of everything upstream. After fixing the notebook, repairing is what gets the workflow to a completed state without paying for the tasks that already succeeded.
Restarting or switching the cluster addresses nothing, because the failure came from the notebook code rather than the compute. Rerunning the whole pipeline would work but repeats successful work.
One wording note: in the Databricks UI the action is called Repair run, and it is initiated from the failed run. On a single-task workflow the distinction is cosmetic, since the one task is the whole run.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/repair-job-failures

question: A data engineer has written a function in a Databricks Notebook to calculate the population of bacteria in a given medium. Analysts use this function in the notebook and sometimes provide input arguments of the wrong data type, which can cause errors during execution. Which Databricks feature will help the data engineer quickly identify if an incorrect data type has been provided as input?
optionA: The Spark User interface has a debug tab that contains the variables that are used in this session.
optionB: The Databricks debugger enables breakpoints that will raise an error if the wrong data type is submitted.
optionC: The Databricks debugger enables the use of a variable explorer to see at a glance the value of the variables.
optionD: The Data Engineer should add print statements to find out what the variable is.
explanation:
Databricks notebooks include a built-in interactive debugger for Python, and the documentation describes what it provides: breakpoints, step-by-step execution and variable inspection. Variable values are shown in the variable explorer pane in the right sidebar, and local variables inside a function appear there marked [local] as you step through it. Seeing the value -- and therefore the type -- of an argument at a glance is exactly how you catch an analyst passing a string where a number was expected.
The old key claimed that breakpoints "will raise an error if the wrong data type is submitted". Breakpoints do no such thing: the documentation is explicit that when the code reaches a breakpoint it stops before the line is run, which is a pause, not a type check. Nothing about a breakpoint validates argument types, so that option describes a mechanism the debugger does not have.
The remaining options are also wrong: the Spark UI has no debug tab holding session variables, and adding print statements is the manual workaround the debugger exists to replace.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/debugger

corrected.note: The debugger documentation lists variable inspection via the variable explorer pane, and states that a breakpoint stops execution before the line runs. The old key attributed type-checking behaviour to breakpoints, which they do not perform -- an invented mechanism rather than a documented one.

question: A data engineer wants to reduce costs and optimize cloud spending. The data engineer has decided to use Databricks Serverless for lowering cloud costs while maintaining existing SLAs. What is the first step in migrating to Databricks Serverless?
optionA: Legacy Ingestion pipelines that include ingestion from sources API's, files, JDBC/ODBC connections
optionB: A frequently running and efficient Python-based data transformation pipeline compatible with the latest Databricks runtime and Unity Catalog
optionC: A frequently running and efficient Scala-based data transformation pipeline compatible with the latest Databricks runtime and Unity Catalog
optionD: Low frequency BI Dashboarding and Adhoc SQL Analytics
explanation:
The workloads that migrate to serverless most safely are the ones already running on a current Databricks Runtime with Unity Catalog, and running often enough that removing cluster start-up time pays back immediately. That points at the frequently running, efficient Python transformation pipeline.
Python rather than Scala matters because serverless carries language-sensitive restrictions: user-defined code including UDFs, map and mapPartitions is capped at 1 GB of memory, Scala UDFs cannot be used inside higher-order functions, and CREATE FUNCTION (External) is unsupported. A Scala-heavy pipeline is therefore likelier to hit a limitation during migration. Low-frequency BI and ad-hoc SQL gain little, since they spend most of their time idle, and legacy ingestion over JDBC/ODBC connections is the most likely to run into the networking constraints.
Treat this item as weakly worded: it asks for a "first step" but every option names a workload rather than a step, and Databricks does not publish a prescribed migration order.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/limitations
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/

corrected.note: Answer stands as the best-supported option. Grounded the Python-over-Scala preference in the documented serverless restrictions on user code, and flagged that the stem asks for a step while the options list workloads -- Databricks publishes no prescribed migration sequence.

question: In order for Structured Streaming to reliably track the exact progress of the processing so that it can handle any kind of failure by restarting and/or reprocessing, which of the following two approaches is used by Spark to record the offset range of the data being processed in each trigger?
optionA: Structured Streaming cannot record the offset range of the data being processed in each trigger.
optionB: Replayable Sources and Idempotent Sinks
optionC: Checkpointing and Write-ahead Logs
optionD: Write-ahead Logs and Idempotent Sinks
optionE: Checkpointing and Idempotent Sinks
explanation:
Spark records streaming progress with checkpointing and write-ahead logs. The offset range being processed in each trigger is written to the checkpoint's log ahead of the batch, so after any failure the engine can identify precisely which range was in flight and restart or reprocess it correctly.
The two options naming idempotent sinks describe the other half of end-to-end exactly-once delivery: replayable sources and idempotent sinks are what let a reprocessed batch land without duplicating output. They are properties of the source and sink rather than the mechanism Spark uses to record offsets, which is what this question asks about.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/structured-streaming/checkpoints

question: A data engineer is working on a personal laptop and needs to perform complex transformations on data stored in a Delta Lake on cloud storage. The engineer decides to use Databricks Connect to interact with Databricks clusters and work in their local IDE. How does Databricks Connect enable the engineer to develop, test, and debug code seamlessly on their local machine while interacting with Databricks clusters?
optionA: By providing a local environment that mimics the Databricks runtime, enabling the engineer to develop, test, and debug code using a specific IDE that is required by Databricks
optionB: By providing a local environment that mimics the Databricks runtime, enabling the engineer to develop, test, and debug code only through Databricks' own web interface
optionC: By allowing direct execution of Spark jobs from the local machine without needing a network connection
optionD: By providing a local environment that mimics the Databricks runtime, enabling the engineer to develop, test, and debug code using their preferred IDE
explanation:
Databricks Connect lets engineers use their preferred local IDE while connecting to Databricks clusters remotely. It mimics the Databricks runtime locally, enabling seamless development, testing, and debugging while executing workloads on the Databricks cluster.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/databricks-connect/

question: A data engineer is working in a Python notebook on Databricks to process data, but notices that the output is not as expected. The data engineer wants to investigate the issue by stepping through the code and checking the values of certain variables during execution. Which tool should the data engineer use to inspect the code execution and variables in real-time?
optionA: Cluster Logs
optionB: Job Execution Dashboard
optionC: Python Notebook Interactive Debugger
optionD: SQL Analytics
explanation:
The Python Notebook Interactive Debugger in Databricks allows stepping through code execution, setting breakpoints, and inspecting variable values in real-time. This makes it the correct tool for debugging Python code inside a Databricks notebook.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/debugger

question: A data engineer is working on a Databricks project that utilizes cloud storage. The data engineer wants to load several JSON files from containers on a storage account as soon as the file arrives within the storage account. Which syntax should the data engineer follow to first load the files into a dataframe and check that it is working as expected using Python?
optionA:
```python
df = spark.read.json("input/path")
```
optionB:
```python
df = spark.readStream.format("cloud").option("json").load("/input/path")
```
optionC:
```python
df = spark.readStream.format("json".load("input/path")
```
optionD:
```python
df = spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles").option("cloudFiles.format", "json").load("/input/path")
```
explanation:
To automatically ingest JSON files as soon as they arrive in cloud storage, the correct syntax is to use Auto Loader with spark.readStream.format("cloudFiles").option("cloudFiles.format",
"json").load("/input/path"). This enables continuous ingestion of new files into a streaming dataframe.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/

question: A data engineer wants to create a relational object by pulling data from two tables. The relational object does not need to be used by other data engineers in other sessions. In order to save on storage costs, the data engineer wants to avoid copying and storing physical data. Which of the following relational objects should the data engineer create?
optionA: Spark SQL Table
optionB: Delta Table
optionC: View
optionD: Database
optionE: Temporary view
explanation:
A temporary view fits both constraints exactly. It stores no data -- it is a saved query evaluated when referenced, so there is no copy and no storage cost -- and it is scoped to the session, which the question explicitly permits since nobody else needs it.
A plain view would also avoid copying data, and is the closest distractor; it is simply broader than needed, persisting in the metastore for other sessions when the requirement says that is unnecessary. A Spark SQL table and a Delta table both materialise and store the data, which is the cost the question is trying to avoid. A database is a container, not a queryable object built from two tables.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/views/

question: A data engineer has inherited a Databricks pipeline from a previous team. The pipeline is missing SLAs and costs more than the allotted budget. On analysis, it is noted that the cluster is not being fully utilized, and the dataset is getting skewed. How should the data engineer resolve this issue?
optionA: Use coalesce() on the dataset to merge partitions and reduce skew.
optionB: Increase the number of executors for the job.
optionC: Repartition the dataset to have it be more optimally spread across all nodes.
optionD: Increase the executor memory for the job.
explanation:
Repartitioning redistributes rows across partitions so the work is spread evenly over the cluster. That directly addresses the two symptoms described: skew means a few partitions hold most of the data, which is also why the cluster looks underused -- most executors finish early and idle while a handful of stragglers run on.
Adding executors or memory scales the cluster up without fixing the imbalance, so the stragglers stay stragglers and the bill grows. coalesce() is the trap: it reduces the partition count without a full shuffle, which makes uneven distribution worse rather than better. Evening out skewed data needs the shuffle that repartition performs.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/

question: A data engineer is configuring a cluster in Databricks and wants to ensure that multiple Spark executors can run tasks concurrently across worker nodes. Which cluster component is responsible for executing tasks?
optionA: Driver
optionB: Notebook
optionC: Executor
optionD: Job scheduler
explanation:
Executors are the processes that run tasks. Each worker node hosts one or more executors, each executor has a number of cores, and Spark schedules one task per core -- so concurrency across the cluster comes from the executors, and adding workers or cores is what raises it.
The driver is the coordinator: it builds the execution plan, splits stages into tasks and hands them out, but it does not run them (a single-node cluster is the exception, where the driver also acts as the worker). The job scheduler decides *when* work runs rather than executing it, and a notebook is an authoring surface.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/spark/

question: A data engineer needs to optimize the data layout and query performance for an e-commerce transactions Delta table. The table is partitioned by "purchase_date" a date column which helps with time-based queries but does not optimize searches on user statistics "customer_id", a high- cardinality column. The table is usually queried with filters on "customer_id" within specific date ranges, but since this data is spread across multiple files in each partition, it results in full partition scans and increased runtime and costs. How should the data engineer optimize the Data Layout for efficient reads?
optionA: Alter table implementing liquid clustering on "customer_id" while keeping the existing partitioning.
optionB: Alter the table implementing liquid clustering by "customer_id" and "purchase_date".
optionC: Alter the table to partition by "customer_id".
optionD: Enable delta caching on the cluster so that frequent reads are cached for performance.
explanation:
Since queries filter by customer_id within purchase_date ranges, partitioning only by purchase_date causes inefficient scans across partitions. The correct optimization is to use Liquid Clustering on both customer_id and purchase_date, which dynamically reorganizes data to optimize for both dimensions and avoids the drawbacks of high-cardinality static partitioning.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/clustering

question: A data engineer needs to provide access to a group named manufacturing-team. The team needs privileges to create tables in the quality schema. Which set of SQL commands will grant a group named manufacturing-team to create tables in a schema named production with the parent catalog named manufacturing with the least privileges?
explanation:
To allow a group to create tables in a schema with least privileges, they need:
- GRANT CREATE TABLE on the schema
- GRANT USE SCHEMA on the schema
- GRANT USE CATALOG on the parent catalog
This ensures proper access without granting unnecessary privileges like creating schemas or catalogs.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

question: A data engineer is implementing a data pipeline using Databricks notebooks. The engineer wants to share parameters such as file paths and processing dates across multiple tasks within a job. Which Databricks utility enables parameter passing?
optionA: display
optionB: dbutils.widgets
optionC: spark.conf
optionD: dbutils.fs
explanation:
dbutils.widgets is the parameter mechanism. Widgets declare named inputs on a notebook, a job task supplies values for them at run time, and the notebook reads them with dbutils.widgets.get -- so the same notebook can be reused across tasks and runs with different file paths and processing dates.
spark.conf is the closest distractor and does hold key-value settings, but it configures a Spark session rather than parameterising a task, and job task parameters are not passed through it. dbutils.fs works with files and display renders output; neither passes parameters.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/notebooks/widgets

question: A new data engineering team team. has been assigned to an ELT project. The new data engineering team will need full privileges on the database customers to fully manage the project. Which of the following commands can be used to grant full permissions on the database to the new data engineering team?
explanation:
GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON DATABASE customers TO team; grants the full set of privileges on the database in one statement, which is what "full permissions" asks for.
The distractors fail on direction, syntax or scope. One inverts the principal and the securable, granting on database team to customers -- the object being granted on comes after ON, the principal being granted to comes after TO. One enumerates privileges but strings them together without commas and misuses the PRIVILEGES keyword. One grants only SELECT, which is read access rather than full control, and names a principal that does not match the group.
One currency note: DATABASE is legacy Hive metastore vocabulary. Under Unity Catalog the equivalent object is a schema, and the same grant reads GRANT ALL PRIVILEGES ON SCHEMA <catalog>.<schema> TO <principal>.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

question: A data engineer is migrating pipeline tasks to reduce operational toil. The workspace used Unity Catalog and is in a region that supports serverless. The engineer wants Databricks to auto-select instance types, manage scaling, apply Photon, and handle runtime upgrades automatically for job runs. How should the data engineer meet this requirement while adhering to Databricks constraints?
optionA: Run the job on a serverless compute for workflows configuration, ensuring Unity Catalog is enabled and regional support is available.
optionB: Use a Pro SQL warehouse and schedule Python notebook tasks to execute as pipeline steps.
optionC: Create a job with a single-task job cluster and manually set instance families and min/max workers.
optionD: Use an all-purpose cluster with cluster policies to enforce standard sizes and enable autoscaling.
explanation:
Serverless compute for workflows allows Databricks to automatically manage instance selection, scaling, Photon enablement, and runtime upgrades for job runs, provided Unity Catalog is enabled and the workspace region supports serverless.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/serverless/

question: A data engineer only wants to execute the final block of a Python program if the Python variable day_of_week is equal to 1 and the Python variable review_period is True. Which of the following control flow statements should the data engineer use to begin this conditionally executed code block?
optionA: if day_of_week = 1 & review_period: = "True":
optionB: if day_of_week == 1 and review_period == "True":
optionC: if day_of_week = 1 and review_period:
optionD: if day_of_week == 1 and review_period:
optionE: if day_of_week = 1 and review_period = "True":
explanation:
Python needs == for comparison and the keyword and for the boolean operator, so the correct line is if day_of_week == 1 and review_period:. Because review_period is already a boolean, testing it directly is the idiomatic form -- no comparison is needed.
The distractors turn on exactly those two characters. Any option using a single = is an assignment, which is a syntax error inside an if. And comparing review_period == "True" tests the boolean against a string, which is False even when the variable is True, since True and "True" are different types. That is the subtle one: it is syntactically valid and still wrong.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: A data engineering team wants to validate a new ingestion pipeline locally while ensuring large aggregations run in serverless compute in their Databricks workspace. They plan to use Databricks Connect and have the option to attach to either a shared cluster or serverless. Which workspace requirement should be confirmed first to avoid connection failures?
optionA: Verify that the workspace has Unity Catalog disabled and the Databricks Connect version is less than the serverless Runtime version.
optionB: Verify that the workspace has Unity Catalog enabled and that the Databricks Connect version supports serverless for the target Runtime release.
optionC: Verify that only assigned access mode clusters are used because serverless is not supported by Databricks Connect.
optionD: Verify that the local Spark version equals the serverless Spark version to satisfy Spark Connect parity.
explanation:
Databricks Connect requires Unity Catalog to be enabled when connecting to serverless compute, and the Databricks Connect version must explicitly support serverless for the target Databricks Runtime to ensure compatibility and prevent connection failures.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/dev-tools/databricks-connect/

question: A data analyst has a series of queries in a SQL program. The data analyst wants this program to run every day. They only want the final query in the program to run on Sundays. They ask for help from the data engineering team to complete this task. Which of the following approaches could be used by the data engineering team to complete this task?
optionA: They could submit a feature request with Databricks to add this functionality.
optionB: They could automatically restrict access to the source table in the final query so that it is only accessible on Sundays.
optionC: They could redesign the data model to separate the data used in the final query into a new table.
optionD: They could only run the entire program on Sundays.
optionE: They could wrap the queries using PySpark and use Python's control flow system to determine when to run the final query.
explanation:
SQL alone has no conditional execution across statements, so the way to run the final query only on Sundays is to drive the queries from Python. Wrapping them with spark.sql() lets ordinary Python control flow decide what runs -- check the weekday, and execute the last query only when it matches.
The alternatives avoid the problem rather than solving it. Running the whole program only on Sundays loses the daily cadence the analyst needs. Restricting table access by day of week enforces the schedule through permissions, which would make the query fail rather than be skipped, and is a fragile way to express timing. Redesigning the data model does not address when a query runs, and submitting a feature request concedes the task is impossible when it is not.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: A data engineer is configuring Unity Catalog in Databricks and needs to assign a role to a user who should have the ability to grant and revoke privileges on various data objects within a specific schema, but should not have read/write access over the schema or its objects. Which role should the data engineer assign to this user?
optionA: Table Owner
optionB: Catalog Owner
optionC: Schema Owner
optionD: USE catalog/schema privilege on the schema
explanation:
The Schema Owner role in Unity Catalog allows a user to grant and revoke privileges on data objects within the schema without requiring read/write access to the schema's data itself, fitting the requirement.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/manage-privileges

question: A data engineer needs to append new records to an existing Delta table while preserving existing data. The ingestion pipeline runs every hour and adds incremental data without replacing previous records. Which write mode should be used?
optionA: append
optionB: errorIfExists
optionC: overwrite
optionD: ignore
explanation:
append adds the new rows and leaves existing data in place, which is what an hourly incremental load needs.
The other three modes each do something the pipeline must not do. overwrite replaces the table's contents, discarding every previously loaded record. errorIfExists -- the default for a DataFrame write -- fails outright once the table exists, so the second hourly run would break. ignore silently does nothing when the table exists, so the pipeline would appear to succeed while loading no data, which is the most dangerous of the three because nothing signals the failure.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-dml-insert-into

question: What is the functionality of AutoLoader in Databricks?
optionA: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling both batch and streaming data with support for schema evolution.
optionB: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling batch and streaming data with no support for schema evolution.
optionC: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling only streaming data with no support for schema evolution.
optionD: Auto Loader automatically ingests and processes new files from cloud storage, handling batch data with support for schema evolution.
explanation:
Auto Loader incrementally ingests new files as they arrive in cloud object storage, and it supports schema evolution -- both halves matter, and only one option states both.
On the batch-versus-streaming point: Auto Loader is built on Structured Streaming and provides the cloudFiles source, but a query using it can be triggered to run periodically rather than continuously. Trigger.AvailableNow processes whatever files have accumulated and then stops, which is how Auto Loader serves scheduled batch ingestion without ceasing to be a streaming source. So it genuinely covers both usage patterns.
On schema evolution: the behaviour is controlled by cloudFiles.schemaEvolutionMode, whose default adds newly discovered columns to the schema, with modes available to rescue unexpected columns, fail on them, or ignore them.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ingestion/cloud-object-storage/auto-loader/schema

question: A data engineer needs to conduct Exploratory Analysis on data residing in a database that is within the company's custom-defined network in the cloud. The data engineer is using SQL for this task. Which type of SQL Warehouse will enable the data engineer to process large numbers of queries quickly and cost-effectively?
optionA: Serverless compute for notebooks
optionB: Pro SQL Warehouse
optionC: Classic SQL Warehouse
optionD: Serverless SQL Warehouse
explanation:
The phrase this question turns on is lifted from the Databricks warehouse-types documentation. Intelligent Workload Management is described there as a set of features that enhances Databricks SQL Serverless's ability to process large numbers of queries quickly and cost-effectively, using AI-powered prediction and dynamic management rather than static thresholds. The feature table lists IWM against Serverless only: Pro gets Photon and Predictive IO, Classic gets Photon alone.
Serverless also starts in roughly two to six seconds and upscales rapidly, so it is the type that absorbs a burst of exploratory queries without paying for idle capacity. Pro and Classic run in the classic compute plane and must spin compute up before answering.
A note on the stem: the reference to a custom-defined network reads as though it should favour a warehouse running inside the customer VPC, but the question asks specifically about processing many queries quickly and cost-effectively, which is the documented IWM wording and therefore Serverless.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/compute/sql-warehouse/warehouse-types

question: What can be used to simplify and unify siloed data architectures that are specialized for specific use cases?
optionA: Delta Lake
optionB: Data lake
optionC: Data warehouse
optionD: Data lakehouse
explanation:
A data lakehouse is a unified architecture that combines the best features of data lakes and data warehouses. It simplifies and unifies siloed data architectures by allowing both structured and unstructured data to coexist in the same system, supporting a wide variety of use cases, such as analytics, machine learning, and business intelligence.
Data lakes are good for storing large amounts of raw data but lack the structure and performance needed for high-performance analytics.
Data warehouses are designed for structured data and analytics but aren't optimized for large volumes of unstructured or semi-structured data.
Delta Lake is a storage layer that brings reliability to data lakes, but a lakehouse is the broader architecture that unifies these approaches.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/

question: A data engineer is standardizing repository layouts for multiple teams adopting Databricks Asset Bundles. The engineer wants to ensure every project has a single authoritative configuration file at the repository root that defines the bundle name, targets, workspace settings, permissions, and resource mappings (for jobs and pipelines). What strategy should the data engineer use to meet the goal?
optionA: Place multiple databricks.ymlfiles under each subfolder (for example, jobs/pipelines/, workspace/) and merge them at deploy time using the include mapping.
optionB: Place exactly one databricks.yml at the repository root; it is the main configuration file and may reference additional configuration files via the include mapping.
optionC: Place a databricks.ymlin a databricks/hidden folder at the repository root; only hidden locations are valid for bundle configs.
optionD: Place a databricks.yaml at the repository root and optional databricks.yml in subfolders; the CLI prefers .yamlover .ymlwhen both exist.
explanation:
Databricks Asset Bundles require a single authoritative databricks.yml file at the repository root that defines core bundle configuration, while allowing modularization by referencing additional files through the include mapping.

question: Which of the following statements regarding the relationship between Silver tables and Bronze tables is always true?
optionA: Silver tables contain more data than Bronze tables.
optionB: Silver tables contain a more refined and cleaner view of data than Bronze tables.
optionC: Silver tables contain less data than Bronze tables.
optionD: Silver tables contain a less refined, less clean view of data than Bronze data.
optionE: Silver tables contain aggregates while Bronze data is unaggregated.
explanation:
The only claim that always holds is that Silver is a more refined and cleaner view of the data than Bronze. That is the definition of the layers: Bronze keeps source data as it arrived, Silver applies cleaning, conforming and deduplication.
Every statement about volume is the trap, because it can go either way. Silver often holds fewer rows than Bronze after deduplication and filtering, but it can hold more columns after joining and enriching, and a Silver table built from several Bronze sources may be larger outright. Neither "more" nor "less" is guaranteed. Aggregation is characteristic of Gold rather than Silver, and the option claiming Silver is less refined inverts the architecture.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

question: A data engineering project involves processing large batches of data on a daily schedule using ETL.
