optionA: Job Cluster
optionB: Dedicated Cluster
optionC: All-Purpose Cluster
optionD: Databricks SQL Serverless
explanation:
Job Clusters are ephemeral clusters created for scheduled or automated workloads. They are cost-efficient, scale automatically to match workload demands, and terminate after job completion, making them the ideal choice for daily large-batch ETL processing.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/compute

question: A data organization leader is upset about the data analysis team's reports being different from the data engineering team's reports. The leader believes the siloed nature of their organization's data engineering and data analysis architectures is to blame. Which of the following describes how a data lakehouse could alleviate this issue?
optionA: Both teams would be able to collaborate on projects in real-time
optionB: Both teams would reorganize to report to the same department
optionC: Both teams would use the same source of truth for their work
optionD: Both teams would autoscale their work as data size evolves
optionE: Both teams would respond more quickly to ad-hoc requests
explanation:
A lakehouse gives both teams one governed copy of the data to work from, which is what removes the disagreement. The reports differed because each team was working from its own extract in its own system; when the engineering pipeline and the analysts' queries read the same tables under the same governance, the numbers reconcile by construction.
The other options describe genuine benefits that do not address this complaint. Real-time collaboration, autoscaling and faster ad-hoc turnaround are all real, but none of them explains why two reports disagree. Reorganising reporting lines is an org change rather than anything a lakehouse does.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/

question: A data engineer wants to read only a subset of columns from a Delta table to reduce memory usage and improve performance. Which Spark DataFrame operation should be used?
optionA: filter
optionB: select
optionC: orderBy
optionD: groupBy
explanation:
select projects a subset of columns, and because Delta stores data in Parquet -- a columnar format -- Spark reads only the files' column chunks it actually needs. That column pruning is what reduces I/O and memory for a wide table.
filter is the close distractor and prunes in the other dimension, removing rows rather than columns; useful, but it does not reduce the number of columns read. orderBy sorts and forces a shuffle, and groupBy aggregates; both add work rather than reducing what is read.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: A data engineer wants to store intermediate data in a temporary view for use within the same Spark session. The data should not persist after the session ends. Which Spark SQL command should be used?
optionA: CREATE TABLE
optionB: CREATE TEMP VIEW
optionC: CREATE VIEW
optionD: CREATE DATABASE
explanation:
CREATE TEMP VIEW registers a view scoped to the current Spark session. It stores no data, it is not written to the metastore, and it disappears when the session ends -- exactly the lifetime the question describes for intermediate results.
CREATE VIEW persists in the metastore and outlives the session, which the question rules out. CREATE TABLE materialises and stores the data, which is more than intermediate results need. CREATE DATABASE makes a container, not a queryable object.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-view

question: A Python file is ready for production and the client wants to use the most efficient yet cost- effective type of cluster possible. The workload is quite small, only processing 10GBs of data with only simple joins and no complex aggregations or wide transformations. Which cluster meets the requirement?
optionA: Job cluster with spot instances enabled
optionB: Job cluster with Photon enabled
optionC: Job cluster with spot instances disabled
optionD: Interactive cluster
explanation:
A job cluster is the most cost-effective option for production workloads because it is created only for the duration of the job and then terminated. Enabling spot instances further reduces cost, and the small, simple workload does not require advanced performance optimizations.

https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/compute

question: A data engineer is configuring a batch processing job in Databricks to read large Parquet datasets from cloud storage. The engineer wants Spark to automatically distribute computation across multiple worker nodes without manually assigning tasks. Which Spark abstraction enables automatic parallel processing?
optionA: Executor
optionB: Cluster
optionC: DataFrame
optionD: Driver
explanation:
The DataFrame is the abstraction that makes parallelism automatic. It represents a distributed collection partitioned across the cluster, and Spark's engine plans the work over those partitions and schedules tasks itself -- so nobody assigns work to nodes by hand.
The other options are parts of the machinery rather than the abstraction. Executors are the processes that run the resulting tasks, the driver plans and coordinates them, and the cluster is the pool of compute they occupy. All are involved, but the DataFrame is what expresses the computation in a form Spark can parallelise.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

The goal is to maintain data security and ensure the partner can access the data efficiently. Which method should the data engineer use to securely share the dataset with the external partner?
optionA: Using Delta Sharing with the open sharing protocol
optionB: Exporting data as CSV files and emailing them
optionC: Using a third-party API to access the Delta table
optionD: Databricks-to-Databricks Sharing

question: A data engineer notices that a Spark job repeatedly scans a large Delta table even though the dataset does not change during the session. Which technique can store the dataset in memory to speed up repeated queries?
optionA: VACUUM
optionB: MERGE
optionC: OPTIMIZE
optionD: CACHE TABLE
explanation:
CACHE TABLE materialises the table into cluster memory, so repeated queries in the same session read from memory instead of rescanning the files. That is the right tool when the data does not change during the session, which the question specifies.
OPTIMIZE is the tempting distractor: it improves read performance, but by compacting small files on disk rather than holding anything in memory, and it rewrites the table rather than caching it. VACUUM deletes unreferenced old files and reclaims storage. MERGE performs conditional upserts. Only one of the four puts data in memory.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-aux-cache-cache-table

question: A data engineer is working with a very large dataset and wants to improve query performance by colocating related data in the same files. The engineer decides to apply Z-ordering on frequently filtered columns. Which Delta Lake command is used?
optionA: ANALYZE TABLE
optionB: CACHE TABLE
optionC: OPTIMIZE ZORDER BY
optionD: VACUUM ZORDER
explanation:
Z-ordering is applied through OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (columns). OPTIMIZE rewrites the table's files, and the ZORDER BY clause decides how rows are colocated within them, so values that are queried together end up in the same files. That improves data skipping, because the per-file statistics in the transaction log then let Spark eliminate far more files for a filtered query.
Z-ordering is not a standalone command, which rules out VACUUM ZORDER. ANALYZE TABLE collects statistics without moving data, and CACHE TABLE holds data in memory without changing its layout.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/data-skipping

question: A data engineer is developing an ETL process based on Spark SQL. The execution fails. The data engineer checks the Spark UI and can see the ERRORS as follows: "java.lang.OutofMemoryError: Java heap space" Which two corrective actions should the data engineer perform to resolve this issue? (Choose two.)
optionA: Narrow the filters in order to collect less data in the query
optionB: Upsize the worker nodes and activate autoshuffle partitions
optionC: Upsize the driver node and deactivate autoshuffle partitions
optionD: Cache the dataset in order to boost the query performance
optionE: Fix the shuffle partitions to 50 to ensure the allocation
explanation:
Reducing input with narrower filters lowers memory pressure, and increasing executor resources (upsize worker nodes) plus enabling adaptive/auto shuffle partitioning provides more memory and better partitioning to avoid Java heap OOM during Spark SQL execution.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/

question: A data engineer is designing an ETL pipeline to process both streaming and batch data from multiple sources. The pipeline must ensure data quality, handle schema evolution, and provide easy maintenance. The team is considering using Delta Live Tables (DLT) in Databricks to achieve these goals. They want to understand the key features and benefits of DLT that make it suitable for this use case. Why is Delta Live Tables (DLT) an appropriate choice?
optionA: Automatic data quality checks, built-in support for schema evolution, and declarative pipeline development
optionB: Manual schema enforcement, high operational overhead, and limited scalability
optionC: Requires custom code for data quality checks, no support for streaming data, and complex pipeline maintenance
optionD: Supports only batch processing, no data versioning, and high infrastructure costs
explanation:
Delta Live Tables (DLT) is appropriate because it provides automatic data quality checks through expectations, built-in support for schema evolution, and a declarative approach to pipeline development, making it easier to build and maintain both streaming and batch ETL pipelines.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/ldp/expectations

question: A data engineer is reading a very large dataset that contains skewed key values. Some partitions contain significantly more records than others, causing uneven workload distribution across executors. Which Spark issue does this scenario describe?
optionA: Schema evolution
optionB: Data skew
optionC: Lazy evaluation
optionD: Broadcast failure
explanation:
This is data skew: the join or grouping key is distributed unevenly, so a few partitions hold far more records than the rest. The visible symptom is exactly what the question describes -- most executors finish quickly and idle while a handful of stragglers carry the bulk of the work, so the stage takes as long as its slowest partition.
The other terms name unrelated concepts. Schema evolution is about a changing schema, lazy evaluation is Spark's deferral of computation until an action is called, and a broadcast failure would concern a table too large to broadcast rather than uneven partitioning.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/optimizations/

question: A data engineer needs to use a Delta table as part of a data pipeline, but they do not know if they have the appropriate permissions. In which location can the data engineer review their permissions on the table?
optionA: Jobs
optionB: Dashboards
optionC: Catalog Explorer
optionD: Repos
explanation:
Catalog Explorer is where a table's permissions are reviewed. Selecting the table shows its owner and the privileges granted on it, which answers whether the engineer already has the access their pipeline needs. Jobs, Dashboards and Repos expose no table-level privilege information.
Catalog Explorer is the current name for what earlier documentation called Data Explorer; a near-duplicate of this question elsewhere in the deck still uses the older label.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/discover/database-objects

question: A data engineer needs to access the view created by the sales team, using a shared cluster. The data engineer has been provided usage permissions on the catalog and schema. In order to access the view created by sales team. What are the minimum permissions the data engineer would require in addition?
optionA: Needs SELECT permission only on the VIEW
optionB: Needs SELECT permission on the VIEW and the underlying TABLE.
optionC: Needs ALL PRIVILEGES on the VIEW
optionD: Needs ALL PRIVILEGES at the SCHEMA level
explanation:
SELECT on the view is enough, provided the engineer can already traverse the catalog and schema, which the question grants. Unity Catalog resolves a view's underlying tables using the *view owner's* privileges, so a reader never needs access to the tables the view reads from. That indirection is what makes views useful for exposing a filtered or masked slice of data without exposing the source.
Requiring SELECT on the underlying table as well is the natural but incorrect assumption, and it would defeat the point of the view. ALL PRIVILEGES on the view or on the schema would work but grants far more than reading requires, which the question rules out by asking for the minimum.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/data-governance/unity-catalog/access-control/privileges-reference

question: A data engineer has a Job that has a complex run schedule, and they want to transfer that schedule to other Jobs. Rather than manually selecting each value in the scheduling form in Databricks, which of the following tools can the data engineer use to represent and submit the schedule programmatically?
optionA: There is no way to represent and submit this information programmatically
optionB: datetime
optionC: pyspark.sql.types.TimestampType
optionD: pyspark.sql.types.DateType
optionE: Cron syntax
explanation:
Job schedules are expressed as cron expressions -- a quartz cron string encodes the minute, hour, day and day-of-week pattern in a single line. Because it is just a string, it can be copied between jobs, stored in a bundle's YAML, or submitted through the Jobs API, which is exactly the transferable, programmatic representation the question asks for.
The Python and Spark type options name ways to represent a single point in time, not a recurring pattern: a timestamp or date value cannot express "every weekday at 06:00". And the claim that no programmatic representation exists is contradicted by the API and the CLI.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/jobs/triggers

question: A data engineer is onboarding a new bronze ingestion pipeline in Databricks with Unity Catalog. The team wants Databricks to handle storage layout, apply platform optimizations over time, and simplify lifecycle management so that when a table is dropped, its underlying data is also cleaned up according to Databricks-managed retention policies. Which table type should the data engineer create for these ingestion tables?
optionA: Managed tables so that Unity Catalog manages both metadata and underlying data lifecycle.
optionB: External tables with a LOCATION pointing to an external volume for full control of file layout.
optionC: Foreign tables federated from an external catalog to delegate optimization to the source system.
optionD: Temporary views over files to avoid table-level governance and lifecycle coupling.
explanation:
Managed tables allow Unity Catalog and Databricks to control both metadata and underlying data storage, enabling automatic optimizations, simplified lifecycle management, and cleanup of data files when tables are dropped according to platform-managed policies.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/managed

question: A data engineer wants to ensure that duplicate records are removed from a dataset based on specific columns before writing to a Delta table. Which Spark DataFrame method removes duplicate rows?
optionA: removeDuplicates
optionB: dropDuplicates
optionC: uniqueRows
optionD: distinctBy
explanation:
dropDuplicates() is the DataFrame method, and it takes an optional list of columns so duplicates can be identified on a subset -- which is what the question asks for. Called without arguments it considers every column, behaving like distinct().
The other three names do not exist in the DataFrame API. That is the whole test here: removeDuplicates, uniqueRows and distinctBy all sound plausible and none of them is real.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/pyspark/

question: Which SQL code snippet will correctly demonstrate a Data Definition Language (DDL) operation used to create a table?
optionA: CREATE TABLE employees ( id INT, name STRING );
optionB: DROP TABLE employees;
optionC: ALTER TABLE employees ADD COLUMN salary DECIMAL(10,2);
optionD: INSERT INTO employees (id, name) VALUES (1 'Alice');
explanation:
CREATE TABLE is a DDL statement: it defines a database object and its schema. That is the category the question asks for, and CREATE TABLE employees (id INT, name STRING); is a well-formed example.
The near-misses are worth separating carefully. DROP TABLE and ALTER TABLE are also DDL -- they define and modify structure too -- but neither *creates* a table, which is what the question specifies. The INSERT statement is the one in a different category entirely: it is DML, operating on rows rather than structure, and as printed it is also malformed, missing the comma between 1 and 'Alice'.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/sql/language-manual/sql-ref-syntax-ddl-create-table-using

question: A data engineer needs to reduce the number of small files generated during streaming ingestion into Delta tables. Small files are causing performance issues during downstream queries. Which Delta Lake feature automatically compacts small files during writes?
optionA: VACUUM
optionB: CACHE
optionC: autoCompact
optionD: OPTIMIZE
explanation:
Auto compaction is the feature that combines small files during writes. Enabled with delta.autoOptimize.autoCompact, it runs after a write commits and rewrites small files into larger ones automatically, which is what keeps streaming ingestion from accumulating thousands of tiny files.
OPTIMIZE is the close distractor: it performs the same compaction but has to be invoked explicitly, as a separate maintenance command, whereas the question asks specifically for automatic compaction during writes. VACUUM removes unreferenced files rather than combining live ones, and CACHE affects memory rather than file layout.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/tables/tune-file-size

question: A data engineering team is using Kafka to capture event data and then ingest it into Databricks. The team wants to be able to see these historical events. Medallion architecture is already in place. The team wants to be mindful of costs. Where should this historical event data be stored?
optionA: Gold
optionB: Silver
optionC: Bronze
optionD: Raw layer
explanation:
In the Medallion architecture, the Bronze layer stores raw ingested data, including historical event data from Kafka. This approach preserves the full history at lower cost while allowing further refinement into Silver and Gold layers.
References:
https://docs.databricks.com/aws/en/lakehouse/medallion

optionA: Repair the task

optionC: Restart the Cluster
